items.title: "Prices Have Just Jumped": Nashville Is Now America’s Unexpected Home Of Ultra-Luxury
items.content_text:
"Prices Have Just Jumped": Nashville Is Now America’s Unexpected Home Of Ultra-Luxury

Nashville is quickly becoming one of America's most desirable cities for business, investment, and luxury living. Once known primarily for country music and entertainment, the Tennessee capital is attracting wealthy individuals, major corporations, entrepreneurs, and professionals from across the country, according to Bloomberg.

Lower taxes, a business-friendly environment, and a high quality of life have helped fuel the city's growth. Many newcomers are relocating from expensive markets like Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York in search of more space, financial advantages, and new opportunities.

Bloomberg writes that major companies are taking notice. Investment firm AllianceBernstein relocated its headquarters from Manhattan to Nashville, while Oracle is developing a major riverfront campus designed to accommodate as many as 8,500 workers. Starbucks is also establishing a growth hub in the city, adding to Nashville's expanding corporate presence.

The real estate market reflects this rising demand. According to Realtor.com data, sales of homes priced among the nation's top 1% tripled in the Nashville metropolitan area between 2017 and 2025. Luxury properties selling for millions of dollars are becoming increasingly common, particularly in Franklin, Brentwood, and surrounding Williamson County.

The region is also attracting celebrities, professional athletes, executives, and high-net-worth families.

Nashville’s growing wealth is changing more than its real estate market. Luxury car dealerships, private clubs, upscale restaurants, and high-end services are expanding to meet demand from affluent newcomers. Just south of the city, 111 Motorcars operates as both an exotic car dealership and private club, storing Porsches, Lamborghinis, and multimillion-dollar vehicles for wealthy clients. 

Some owners maintain collections worth tens of millions of dollars, with staff handling everything from maintenance to transportation. “They want no friction,” co-founder Jeremy Scates said. “They want everything to be easy and on a silver platter.”

The region’s luxury housing market is equally impressive. In Franklin and surrounding Williamson County, sprawling estates, gated compounds, and multimillion-dollar mansions are attracting buyers seeking privacy, acreage, and proximity to Nashville. 

Recent listings have included a $34.8 million estate spanning more than 122 acres, a $19.5 million property featuring a historic recording studio, and a $33.5 million penthouse at the Four Seasons in downtown Nashville. Some properties have seen extraordinary appreciation. 

“Prices have just jumped,” said luxury real estate agent Jamie Parsons to Bloomberg, who described one property that sold for $6 million in 2021 and more than $18 million in 2026.

Beyond the mansions and luxury cars, Nashville continues to attract residents through its established music industry, expanding corporate presence, Vanderbilt University, and access to Tennessee’s scenic countryside. Affluent newcomers can enjoy the amenities of a growing city while living on large private estates just miles from downtown.

However, the influx of wealth is also driving up housing and land prices, making it increasingly difficult for longtime residents and younger families to remain in the area. Rising development pressures are also raising concerns about the future of the region’s farmland and historic rural communities.

Despite these challenges, Nashville’s transformation is undeniable. Once primarily associated with country music and entertainment, Music City is becoming a destination for billionaires, business executives, professional athletes, and luxury buyers seeking a different lifestyle.

items.title: University Of San Francisco Caves To Wokeness, Cancels Mascot After 90 Years
items.content_text:
University Of San Francisco Caves To Wokeness, Cancels Mascot After 90 Years

Authored by Bryan Hyde via American Greatness,

The University of San Francisco (USF) has officially announced that its new mascot is the wolf, replacing the nearly century-old "Don" costume following student backlash over colonial history.

The New York Post reports that the school announced Friday that "The Don" - a costumed figure sporting a pencil mustache and a green Spanish-style hat - will officially step aside at the start of the spring 2027 semester.

While the university is completely retiring the costumed character "The Don" ahead of the spring 2027 semester, athletic teams will proudly retain the "Dons" nickname, according to the San Francisco Chronicle.

Sounds like a lame April Fool's joke but instead just another example of extremely weak university leadership. 400 signatures on a petition? 🤣
@USFDonsAD and @DonsAthletics you're an embarrassment.
https://t.co/DTzSkZkh1t

— mike hiserman (@MikeHiserman) November 2, 2026

The mascot originally honored Don Francisco de Haro, the first mayor of Yerba Buena before it became San Francisco.

The figure sparked widespread debate in 2022 when USF's student government passed a formal resolution demanding its removal, arguing the character symbolized the exploitation and subjugation of California's indigenous people.

SFist reports critics argued that the traditional figure - characterized by a mask, pencil mustache, and a green Spanish-style hat - glorified colonial history and Spanish expansion.

The decision to remove the mascot followed years of student-led petitions and government resolutions targeting "The Don", a Spanish honorific which translates to "of noble origin."

USF President Salvador Aceves described the transition as a natural evolution, saying:

With new leadership at USF and in Dons Athletics, we believe the time is right to revitalize our image and embrace a new mascot, one that is known for its intelligence, endurance and ability to work cooperatively in its pack. At the same time, we will proudly remain the University of San Francisco Dons.

"The Don" mascot (which originally debuted in 1932) is stepping down at the conclusion of the fall 2026 term, with the official rollout of the wolf character commencing at the start of the spring 2027 semester.

The decision sparked mixed reactions across the university community, with several alumni venting their frustration online and accusing the administration of unnecessarily rewriting decades of campus sports history.

items.title: Iran Proves Willingess To Re-Engage In Nuclear Talks, Despite Public Stance: NYT
items.content_text:
Iran Proves Willingess To Re-Engage In Nuclear Talks, Despite Public Stance: NYT

Update(1219ET): Tehran has made clear it will not stop the war, or the assaults on internatinal shipping in the Strait Of Hormuz, unless its 'seven conditions' are met. It has also said time and again that the nuclear file is an issue for future, post-war negotiations.

But a fresh report in the NY Times suggests that progress is being made on nuclear enrichment. While the report is perhaps dubious - given the number of times the claim of 'progress in talks' has been floated:

Iran is reviewing a set of proposals presented by mediators that could shape the future of its nuclear program, according to five officials briefed on the negotiations, representing a potential breakthrough in stalled diplomatic efforts to end its war with the United States.

Iran’s willingness to re-engage in nuclear talks, after weeks of refusing to budge, suggests recent mediation efforts led by Qatar to prevent a return to full-blown war have had some success, the officials said. They described the terms being reviewed as “concrete proposals,” without elaborating.

The Iranian foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The five officials, including an American and two Iranians, spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details of the talks.

Qatar has spearheaded a diplomatic blitz with Iran in the past week, the officials added, participating in two rounds of talks in Tehran and hosting a third in Doha. Two of them said that the Qataris have also held recent talks with Iranian officials in Armenia.

The NYT Times headline has resulted in oil prices fall lower on Thursday.

* * *

In a significant albeit underreported development for global energy, and for the US-Iran standoff in the Persian Gulf, Iranian parliament has this week announced it is exempting several key trading partniers from its oil transit restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz.

The move was first unvieled Tuesday by Ahmad Hayat-Moghaddam, Vice Chairman of the Iranian Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, at a moment Iranian export flows are struggling under the many months-long US naval blockade of the country's ports.

"We have currently exempted India, China, Iraq and Qatar from transit restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz. Ships from these countries pass freely," Hayat-Moghaddam stated in an interview to the Iranian Student’s News Agency (SNA).

He described that this also aimed at shoring up "mutual interests" among countries that have long done business with one another.

The Iranian official also sought to frame the change as arising out of joint humanitarian concerns:

Tehran is facilitating the movement of Indian ships for the purpose of medicines, while Chinese ships are exempted from the restrictions to “secure” Beijing’s political support, Hayat-Moghaddam told SNA.

His comments suggested further that the US Navy doesn't block these ships from passing, which could explain how Iran has continued to get oil and wares out to global markets despite the blockade. "The Americans do not interfere with them either," he claimed.

According to more of the remarks:

Elaborating on the rationale behind the decision, the lawmaker noted that the Islamic Republic does not levy transit tolls on Qatari vessels and that each exemption was granted based on specific considerations and agreements. Hayat-Moghaddam remarked: “We are conducting business, and each of these exemptions has a distinct reason.”

According to the MP, India’s exemption was designed to facilitate medicine imports into Iran, while China’s exemption aims to secure political backing from Beijing for the Islamic Republic.

October saw a record number of attacks on commercial vessels by Iran, keeping geopolitical risk elevated across the region; however, what was a near-daily pace of the attacks seems to have slowed, for now.

Even global media reporting has slowed in terms of an Iranian focus, having given way to the midterm elections and major Democratic gains in the US.

President Trump has still held off on prior threats to resume a major bombing campaign after the midterm elections - but this is a possibility still on the table. The Democratic sweep and impending control of the House and Senate might perhaps make renewed major war a more distant possibility.

items.title: Luigi's Cousin Wins A Seat, And His Opponent Won't Concede
items.content_text:
Luigi's Cousin Wins A Seat, And His Opponent Won't Concede

Nino Mangione, a Republican first cousin of accused UnitedHealthcare CEO killer Luigi Mangione, won a seat on the Baltimore County Council on Tuesday, taking about 49% of the vote to 45% for Democrat Shawn McIntosh in District 5, according to unofficial results compiled by the Maryland Association of Counties.

Independent Cory Shaffer drew just over 2,000 votes, while WYPR put Mangione's lead over McIntosh at about 1,200 votes. The race isn't over on paper: McIntosh has not conceded and is waiting on mail-in ballots, as are two other Democratic council candidates who trailed on election night, WYPR reported. Official results come after a full count of pending votes.

Mangione, 39, served in the Maryland House of Delegates from 2019 to 2026. The county Republican central committee appointed him to the council in late May to finish the term of Wade Kach, who resigned, and he resigned his House seat when he was sworn in on June 1. He then won the June 23 Republican primary, taking 75% against riverkeeper Theaux Le Gardeur, according to the same county wrap-up.

His win comes as the council grows from seven seats to nine. Democrats are expected to hold a 5-4 majority on the new council, with Republicans winning Mangione's seat along with David Marks, Josh Sines and Tim Fazenbaker, per the unofficial tally.

The Cousin Nobody Talks About

Nino Mangione has kept his distance from the case. After Luigi's December 2024 arrest he issued a statement for the family expressing shock and sympathy for the Thompson family, and he has declined to answer questions about his cousin since.

That case has since reached a different place than the campaign. Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court in August to the stalking charges tied to the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, telling the judge, "I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan," as we reported. The plea left his state murder case alive on paper, where he has pleaded not guilty; his lawyers are expected to argue it should be dismissed on double jeopardy grounds, which we covered when the plea came in.

Voters in District 5 knew the name. It is the same last name on the ballot as the man whose face became a symbol for the anger at health insurers, and a Republican with it still carried the district by four points in a midterm year when his party lost badly elsewhere.

items.title: Epstein-Linked Billionaire Just Sued The Congressman About To Run The Oversight Committee
items.content_text:
Epstein-Linked Billionaire Just Sued The Congressman About To Run The Oversight Committee

Billionaire Leon Black filed a federal defamation suit Wednesday against Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, accusing him of lying about Black's ties to Jeffrey Epstein. The complaint, filed in the Southern District of New York, seeks $7.25 million in compensatory and punitive damages and a jury trial, and alleges Garcia "has knowingly and willfully lied about Leon Black and defamed him," NBC News reported.

Black undoubtedly had this ready to go after midterms - as following Tuesday's blue tsunami, Democrats will take control of the House in January, and Garcia is expected to become Oversight chairman. This would put him in charge of the committee that has already subpoenaed Black and voted to hold him in contempt.

According to the suit, Garcia said in a television interview weeks after Black's June voluntary interview with the committee that Black "is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein's crimes" and was "one of the last people to actually interact" with Epstein before his death in prison. The complaint also cites Garcia saying he had spoken with survivors who named Black as involved in direct abuse of women. Black's lawyers say the statements were false and malicious, and that they caused "real and significant ongoing harm": threats to his physical safety, a stream of hateful calls, emails and posts, and damage to his business and philanthropic work. 

A Black spokesperson said he has never abused a woman, has never been with an underage woman, has never been involved in sex trafficking and never paid Epstein for women.

The suit is the second Black has filed over the Epstein case. In early September he defied the committee's subpoena and sued the panel and its Republican chairman, Rep. James Comer, calling the probe a "public fishing expedition." Garcia answered that day that Black had "funded Epstein's abuse and trafficking of women" and that "multiple women have also accused Black of sexual assault." Black had left his June interview before it finished, then skipped a later deposition. The committee voted unanimously in September to hold him in contempt, and the full House followed. The Justice Department said on Sept. 16 that the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia "will review the referral of Mr. Black carefully." No charges have been filed against Black.

The money is the center of the dispute. Lawmakers allege Black paid Epstein $180 million. An Apollo-commissioned review in 2021 found $158 million in payments from 2012 to 2017, which it said were for tax, estate planning and related services. Black, who co-founded Apollo Global Management, stepped down as its CEO in 2021 after that review; it found he was not involved in Epstein's criminal activities, and he has denied wrongdoing.

Black has been on the defensive in court for years. items.title: Russell Brand Found Guilty As 'Only Three Rapes' Defense Fails
items.content_text:
Russell Brand Found Guilty As 'Only Three Rapes' Defense Fails

Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault, three days after his barrister asked jurors, "Why is it that only three rapes in 10 years?"

The 51-year-old comedian was convicted at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday of one count of rape and three of sexual assault, the Telegraph reported. The rape conviction relates to a young fan Brand met after one of his Hammersmith Apollo shows in 2009, and one of the sexual assaults to a woman at a Soho bar in 2004, according to GB News.

Brand had faced seven counts involving six women between 1999 and 2009, and pleaded not guilty to all of them. Reports did not immediately say whether the jury cleared him of the remaining three counts - two of rape and one of attempted indecent assault - or is still considering them.

Brand, who was accompanied to court by his wife Laura Gallacher, is expected to face a lengthy prison sentence.

As we reported on Wednesday, Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC, closed the defense on Monday by turning his client's sex life into an argument for acquittal. "What matters is he had an immense amount of sex and none of it was unlawful," Winter told the jury of eight men and four women, which began deliberating on Tuesday.

Megyn Kelly, recapping the closing on her show, put the argument more bluntly: "He had a goal of 5,000, three women, three say he didn't consent out of 5,000. If this guy's running around just randomly raping women orally, vaginally, anally, wouldn't there be more?"

The 5,000 was never a count of partners. A former friend, Mark Pinheiro, testified that Brand once told him of an ambition to sleep with 5,000 women, which Brand denied on the stand: "No, not a goal."

Winter also told jurors the women "all came forward for reasons connected to the TV programme," arguing that the 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches investigation had "poisoned the well of justice." Scotland Yard opened its investigation in September 2023 after that program and the Sunday Times aired allegations from several women, and Brand was charged in April 2025 with five offenses against four women, all between 1999 and 2005.

The rape he was convicted of was not among those original charges. More women came forward after the publicity, and on Dec. 23 prosecutors added one count of rape and one of sexual assault, both from 2009, involving two more women.

Brand presented on BBC Radio 2 from 2006 until 2008, when he quit over his prank calls to actor Andrew Sachs, and the Telegraph noted the verdict adds to pressure on the BBC over how it policed its stars, after the Huw Edwards scandal and the Jimmy Savile affair.

Since leaving mainstream TV, Brand converted to Christianity, reinvented himself as an anti-establishment commentator and insisted the charges were politically motivated. Elon Musk publicly backed him when the allegations surfaced in 2023, and last year Tucker Carlson called on the Trump administration to "rescue" Brand from charges he described as "political and absurd," Variety reported.

Kelly broke with that camp from the start. When the allegations first aired, she told her listeners: "Could you please for a second stay open minded to the possibility that the women are telling the truth?"

items.title: Hormuz Oil Flows Unlikely To Return To Pre-War Levels, Rystad Says
items.content_text:
Hormuz Oil Flows Unlikely To Return To Pre-War Levels, Rystad Says

Authored by Michael Kern via OilPrice,

The United States and Iran could reach some form of a limited agreement by the middle of 2027, which would allow oil flows from the Strait of Hormuz to continue to gradually recover, but fundamental differences will remain, and the Middle East situation will remain far from normal next year, according to Rystad Energy.

"Achieving a comprehensive settlement would require addressing issues related to Iran's nuclear program, sanctions, Tehran-backed armed groups in the region, and the security of maritime shipping, while also taking into account Israel's security interests," Rystad Energy said in a report cited by Azeri news agency Trend.

"We consider it unlikely that all these points of contention can be resolved within the coming year," the analysts led by Rystad's Head of Geopolitical Analysis, Jorge León, wrote in the report.

Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz will continue to recover gradually, but are unlikely to reach pre-war levels in a normalized trade flow, according to the energy intelligence firm.

Rystad Energy has estimated that crude oil exports from Persian Gulf producers averaged nearly 12 million barrels per day (bpd) in September and the first 20 days of October.

"While this is well above the lows recorded earlier in the conflict, it remains substantially below the pre-war level of approximately 18 million barrels per day," the report reads.

While flows have recovered substantially from the lows in the spring, the security situation in and near the Strait of Hormuz has actually deteriorated, with a higher number of attacks on tankers in recent weeks, according to Rystad Energy.

In the near term, the risk of renewed military escalation following the U.S. midterm elections could be another setback to the recovering Hormuz oil flows, although President Trump has said that he is no hurry to .

items.title: Paraguay's President Resigns Amid Ueno Bank Crisis, Millions Of Depositors In The Streets
items.content_text:
Paraguay's President Resigns Amid Ueno Bank Crisis, Millions Of Depositors In The Streets

Update (1100ET): Under massive pressure from millions in the streets, Paraguay’s President Santiago Peña has signed his resignation letter amid Ueno Bank crisis, local news outlet ABC reported without clarifying how it obtained the information.

The turmoil marks a tectonic shift within the Colorado Party, which propelled Peña to power in 2023. Divided into rival factions, the party has dominated Paraguayan politics for most of the past seven decades.

Congress kicked off discussions to impeach the president Thursday morning, when Horacio Cartes, the powerful former president and leader of the ruling Colorado Party, which holds a majority in congress, publicly backed his ouster.

~~~~

Paraguay's central bank seized Ueno Bank on Tuesday, locking an estimated 3 million customers out of their money and setting off street protests and an impeachment bid against President Santiago Peña. The central bank's board voted unanimously late Monday to put the digital lender into "resolution," the regulator announced, after Ueno's solvency ratio fell below half the legal minimum. Customers could not withdraw or transfer a guaraní.

Ueno says its customers number about 3 million, roughly 60% of Paraguay's adult population, though Paraguayan press counts put the number of account holders nearer 1.7 million. It was also holding between $800 million and $850 million in public money, including about $380 million from the state pension and health fund, known as IPS. The central bank's own criminal complaint alleges that Ueno made large unsecured loans to companies inside its own corporate group and used new borrowing to cover repeated overdrafts, and describes an allegedly simulated $74.4 million sale of loans meant to hide that exposure, according to Diario HOY.

#BREAKING Paraguay's largest digital bank Ueno COLLAPSES

Central Bank seizes it after solvency ratio crashes and around 3 million customers are LOCKED OUT of app, cards & transfers.

Central Bank President Carlos Carvallo resigned right after pulling the plug. He previously ran... pic.twitter.com/A1LZsS1pLz

— Global OSINT (@GlobalOSINTHQ) November 5, 2026

The political problem is that Peña was a business partner of Ueno's owners until March 2025. The bank belongs to Grupo Vázquez, and Peña held shares in its holding company until an extraordinary shareholders' assembly cancelled his stake that month. He said in April 2025 that he was never a shareholder or investor in the bank itself, and Ueno says the same. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo to run the central bank in 2023, after Carvallo had chaired Ueno's predecessor, Financiera Ueno, until mid-2023. The central bank says Carvallo recused himself from every Ueno decision.

The warnings were not hidden. In June the central bank told Ueno it was lending too much to companies tied to its owners. In September the regulator opened an administrative investigation, and senators from Peña's own Colorado Party and the opposition began demanding that he replace the bank's leadership. On Oct. 29, the same day a central bank board member, economist Carmen Marín, resigned, Ueno announced a $100 million capital plan. Fitch had already moved its outlook on the bank to negative. Peña, for his part, repeatedly dismissed concerns about Ueno's finances and accused the media of fearmongering.

Once the bank went under, the central bank's own president became the first casualty. Peña said he asked Carvallo to resign. Carvallo said he had signed his resignation but would stay to oversee the takeover, because "the central bank needs calm to do its job." Peña has nominated Raúl Vera Bogado to replace him, subject to congressional approval.

Prosecutors ordered the arrest of eight people, including Ueno President Juan Manuel Gustale and chief executive Federico Miguel Vázquez Villasanti, and by Tuesday afternoon two more directors were in custody. By Wednesday evening a judge had accepted charges against 27 people, and prosecutors asked for pretrial detention for principal shareholder Miguel Vázquez and house arrest for seven other detained executives. Hearings for the eight were set for Thursday. Adjustments to Ueno's accounts exposed a shortfall of more than 1.6 trillion guaraníes (about $260 million) in funds set aside for losses, and the bank admitted it could not replenish $70 million in required reserves, per ABC Color.

Depositors took to the streets within hours. On Wednesday, a second day of protests, hundreds of savers, retirees, students and workers filled central Asunción near the Panteón de los Héroes, ABC Color reported. They demanded the immediate removal of Peña and Vice President Pedro Alliana. 

"We demand the immediate removal of the President and the Vice President," one protester said [translated], adding that "this is not going to end today." 

Another told the paper: "They hit the people's pocket and we cannot allow that."

Police used a water cannon and tear gas near Congress after what they said was an attempt to breach a security barrier, according to Última Hora. Some protesters said they would spend the night in the plaza next to the legislature.

Opposition lawmakers filed an impeachment request against Peña backed by 35 signatures, accusing him of conflicts of interest and failures of oversight and citing both his stake in Ueno's holding company and the Carvallo appointment. The Chamber of Deputies scheduled an extraordinary session for Thursday at 10 a.m. to take it up, with a separate request against Alliana to follow. That is a long shot, since Peña's Colorado Party controls both chambers, but dissident Colorado legislators are among those who presented it, and one of the party's vice presidents has called for Peña's expulsion. The presidency denied rumors Wednesday night that he was resigning.

Peña canceled a trip to an international summit in Spain, promised that "those responsible will have to answer to the courts, without exceptions or privileges," and agreed with congressional leaders to fast-track a law to speed payouts. A central bank guarantee fund covers up to about $38,000 per person, which preliminary estimates say fully protects roughly 97% of Ueno's depositors. Above that, the regulator has promised only "the greatest possible protection." Senate President Basilio Núñez, who has defended Peña and blamed the central bank, acknowledged that the Senate's first version of the law included a provision that cannot work while Ueno is in resolution, and the text is being amended.

The state pension fund says pensions will be paid as usual. IPS is moving about 32,000 retirees who collect through Ueno to another bank and plans legal action to recover its money. BNO's local sources put its exposure at about $355 million, 9% of its investment portfolio, a figure that differs from the roughly $380 million other reports give.

The collapse also impacts the narrative that Paraguay has been peddling to investors. The landlocked country won its first investment-grade ratings only recently on low taxes, light regulation and stability. It also ranked 150th of 182 countries in Transparency International's 2025 corruption index, tied with Bangladesh and the Central African Republic. Peña cannot seek reelection in 2028, and the crisis has already deepened a succession fight inside his party: Alliana had conditioned his own candidacy on the central bank clearing up doubts about the financial system.

items.title: Nintendo Switch 2 Sales Plunge Amid Memory Crisis; Bernstein Calls It "Not A Good Result"
items.content_text:
Nintendo Switch 2 Sales Plunge Amid Memory Crisis; Bernstein Calls It "Not A Good Result"

Nintendo Switch 2 sales came in materially below Wall Street expectations. Second quarter earnings showed a 41% decline in sales as price increases, shortages, and the memory crisis weighed on demand

The Kyoto-based gaming company sold 2.67 million consoles in the three months ended Sept. 30, down from 3.82 million in the previous quarter. Nintendo hiked prices in the US, Canada, and Japan as a global memory chip shortage drove up component costs. 

Revenue for the quarter totaled $2.8 billion, below the $3.04 billion average analyst estimate compiled by LSEG. Net income of $464.4 million missed expectations of $519.2 million

Morningstar equity director Kazunori Ito wrote earlier, "The slowdown has arrived earlier than anticipated," adding, "It's clear that investors have cooled on the Switch 2 platform."

Nintendo maintained its forecast of 16.5 million Switch 2 consoles for the fiscal year ending March 2027. 

Kantan Games CEO Serkan Toto told CNBC that Nintendo needs more blockbuster games to sustain momentum and win over consumers. This comes as Grand Theft Auto VI is set to debut in the coming weeks.

Bernstein gaming analyst Robin Zhu offered his first take on the earnings:

Nintendo Q2: The memory hit lands

A whiff mostly on hardware margins. Nintendo's Q2 results came in materially below street expectations. Revenue (JPY448bn) fell 15.0% year on year against comps from immediately after the Switch 2 launch, but was in-line with our estimate and consensus. JPY73.9bn of operating profit meanwhile was lower than both our modeling (JPY92.4bn) and street consensus (JPY88.1bn). 2.68mn of Switch 2 hardware units sold in Q2 compared with us and the street on c. 3mn units. 47.0mn software units meanwhile was close to our modelling on c. 47.3mn units, with mix tilted slightly more in favour of Switch 2

7% hardware gross margins? In a way, we'd argue that a miss driven by memory cost headwinds is somehow… less bad than (as some Nintendo bears had argued for) if software units or revenues had disappointed. Hardware ARPU as reported came to JPY68.1k/$430 in Q2, compared with the JPY65.5k/$415 we'd modelled. JPY195bn of software revenue was slightly short versus our JPY200bn estimate, though blended billings per unit (grossing third-party games up to a 100% basis) of JPY6,300/$40 was actually a little higher than the JPY5,500/$35 we'd modelled. Sales of first-party titles like Rhythm Heaven Groove and Fire Emblem Fortune's Weave fell slightly short versus our prior estimates, but third party was able to offset

Not a good result, but… Nintendo's shares fell c. 7% after hours, which feels… reasonable. Qualitative expectations into the quarter were muted for the most part, and our sense is most investors have turned their attention to how many million units Ocarina of Time Remake sells in the coming weeks, and whether Mario joins the line-up this time next year. Both the 1998 Ocarina of Time and 2011 3DS remake saw c. 20% attach rates at launch, but we'd argue the real significance of the 2026 Remake is that it gives the Switch 2 a first (or second, if one includes Mario Kart World, bundled at launch) must-play game which should sell millions beyond the first year. The latter remains a waiting game, though Nintendo has sounded more constructive on tent-pole releases of late

Nintendo shares in Tokyo have been halved since late 2025 as rising chip costs have pressured hardware margins and forced Switch 2 price increases. The following sales slowdown suggests that some consumers may be at the upper limits of what they're willing to pay not just for the handheld console but games too. 

An overlay of "memory shortage" headlines tracked through Bloomberg's NT function and Nintendo's share price shows the stock's bear market coinciding with increased coverage of the shortage. 

Unless Democrats pop the AI bubble with nationwide moratoriums, the memory shortage will linger well into next year.

Mike Johnson To Step Down As Top House Republican After Election Loss

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is no longer going to be the top Republican in the House soon.

Johnson will not run to be the Republican House leader in the next Congress, a spokesman told The Epoch Times in an email on Nov. 4.

Johnson, 54, has been House speaker since 2023 and won another term representing Louisiana's Fourth Congressional District. Johnson said it has been an honor serving as the 56th House speaker and later added that he is optimistic about the future.

"Republicans will not be deterred by the outcome of one election. In fact, you know what we do? We double down. We double down. All right," he said. Among the options to succeed Johnson will be Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), who told GOP colleagues on Wednesday that he will run for the top Republican post.

"For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democrat majority," Jordan wrote in a letter.

He noted that Democrats have pledged to investigate administration officials.

"I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats' playbook," Jordan said. "I know what it will take to lead our Conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the Democrats' tactics. We need a Leadership team that is active and engaged, forward-thinking and straight-shooting."

Jordan has tried several times to become the top Republican in the House, but failed

items.title: Pandemonium In Europe's Skies: Wave Of Bomb Threats Triggers Emergency Landings, Fighter Jet Intercepts
items.content_text:
Pandemonium In Europe's Skies: Wave Of Bomb Threats Triggers Emergency Landings, Fighter Jet Intercepts

A slew of bomb threats against European airlines has resulted in mass reroutings and flight delays over European skies and at major hubs, amid a scramble to find out who is making these threats.

"At least 18 commercial flights in Europe had to deal with bomb threats Thursday, with at least one being diverted to a military base in France," CBS reports of the developing Thursday incidents.

"While authorities have reported no explosives discovered on any of the jets, and they all appeared to be hoaxes, Thursday's incidents add to a fast-growing number of journeys hit by similar threats this week," the report continues.

Some are calling it a "very deliberate act" - which seems coordinated to sow panic and flight disruptions. But authorities have come up with no workable theories or links to any entity behind it so far.

Earlier this week, security officials in the UK deemed that threats against about seven flights were hoaxes. By Thursday these 'hoax' threats had impacted at least 25 flights, disrupting travel for thousands.

And in some cases flights have had to be diverted midair. An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome early in the afternoon of Thursday had to land at a military air bace in France, the French government confirmed. Bomb units investigated the plane upon landing, after all 151 passengers and six crew members safely disembarked.

Based on CBS and international reporting, the below is a list of impacted or diverted flights thus far on Thursday:

  • Ireland–Italy Aer Lingus: Diverted to Evreux air base in France following a bomb threat; 157 passengers and crew deplaned safely for military inspection.
  • Finnair Flights: A Helsinki–Rome flight was escorted by fighter jets to Rome, briefly grounding airport operations, while a second Helsinki flight landed normally in Vienna.
  • Wizz Air Flights: Threat reports forced a Milan–Warsaw flight to reroute to Vienna and prompted security checks on a Bucharest-bound flight after a safe landing.
  • LOT Polish Airlines: A Warsaw–Brussels flight landed safely in Belgium, where security sweeps cleared the aircraft of any hazards.
  • Bulgarian Diverted Flights: Three Sofia-bound Ryanair flights made emergency landings across Bulgaria due to threat alerts; no explosives were found.
  • Prague Inbound Threats: Four incoming flights landed safely in the Czech capital and were cleared by police after security evaluations.
  • Milan Malpensa Inbound: Two flights from Thessaloniki and Porto landed safely following bomb alerts and underwent explosive inspections without diverting.
  • Madrid Barajas Threats: Three flights were impacted by bomb threats, but security forces quickly cleared all aircraft and ruled out the threats.

To be expected, some European media reports are immediately pointing the finger at Russian intelligence or proxies and 'hybrid warfare'. 

The Guardian highlights the large geographic scope of the hoaxes and threats, writing:

Bomb threats have caused diversions and emergency landings for at least 15 flights across Europe, renewing questions about a possibly coordinated effort to disrupt travel.

The series of warnings on Thursday morning affected flights between Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, Greece and Czechia.

On Tuesday seven planes across Europe were searched or diverted because of malicious hoax bomb alerts. On Monday a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted after a threat that was apparently without substance.

Flight map source:

The reports speculates that "simply creating disruption could be regarded as a success by those carrying out the hoaxes."

Likely as European security officials move into the investigative phase, there will be more and more finger-pointing at Russia or its allies, for example Belarus. However, at this early point European media has stressed that "Initial searches of some of the planes found nothing suspicious." Interestingly, almost all of the cases involved budget or low-cost carriers.

items.title: Life After AI: Where The Money Is Now Moving
items.content_text:
Life After AI: Where The Money Is Now Moving

Submitted by QTR's Fringe Finance

As I write this Thursday morning, Dow futures are green while Nasdaq futures are down roughly 0.5%. It’s a small but interesting divergence, and one that supports something I’ve been predicting for a while now: a rotation away from speculative technology and AI-related investments and toward established businesses with more predictable earnings and cash flows.

I continue to believe tech, particularly the more speculative corners of the AI trade, is headed lower over the short to medium term. Yesterday’s rally didn’t change that view. As I discussed yesterday, citing Gordon Johnson, I think much of the move could be attributable to VIX compression and the unwinding of election-related hedges. Once the election uncertainty disappeared, investors no longer needed as much protection, implied volatility fell, and the resulting repositioning helped push stocks higher.

That doesn’t mean there wasn’t genuine buying, or that the market can’t rally further. But I would be careful about mistaking a mechanical relief rally for a fundamental improvement in the outlook. Valuations remain stretched, financing costs remain a problem, and the economics of the AI infrastructure boom are increasingly difficult to justify. The election, in my opinion, added another layer of risk rather than removing one.

What interests me more than yesterday’s index performance is where money appears to be moving to.

For a few months, I’ve been arguing that 2027 could be characterized by a rotation away from speculative AI and technology investments and toward larger, established companies with real earnings and durable businesses.

The relative action in some names I’ve pointed out, including Nike (NKE), Costco (COST) Microsoft (MSFT), Uber (UBER), Consumer Staples (VDC) and McDonald’s (MCD), along with several other companies I’ve been watching, suggests that process may already be underway. Names like these are outperforming the NASDAQ and that outperformance appeared to accelerate during yesterday’s rally.

These businesses have very different exposures, but they share an important characteristic: investors can evaluate them based on existing operations and identifiable earnings power, rather than exclusively on extraordinary assumptions about future growth.

Microsoft, for example, may face legitimate questions about its AI spending, but it has the financial resources to fund those ambitions without continually returning to capital markets.

Interestingly, JPMorgan’s trading desk described a similar pattern yesterday. According to an X post by Zero Hedge, JPM’s Brian Heavey noted a clear preference for large-cap quality, particularly companies with access to financing and ownership of computing infrastructure. The desk observed demand for hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet, while second-tier AI infrastructure names like CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS), which are more dependent on continued capital raising, showed weakness.

As I noted on a brief X Spaces call yesterday, names with leverage (like CoreWeave) and inconsistent cash flows will be the first to be abandoned in the AI space. Quality like Google (GOOG), Amazon (AMZN) and the likes will be the beneficiaries, though I personally don’t love Apple (AAPL) here at 40x earnings.

JPMorgan also noted that AI data-center names were generally underperforming, while more cyclical analog semiconductor companies like Texas Instruments (TXN) and NXP Semiconductors (NXPI) were showing relative strength.

Matt Reiner, also from JPMorgan, described relatively subdued trading activity, with volumes running approximately 16% below normal early in the session today.

Long-only investors were buying, particularly cyclicals, while hedge funds were shorting technology into weakness. He also observed that investors were adding mega-cap technology exposure in relatively small size, while becoming more receptive to shorting the broader AI complex.

To me, the message is fairly straightforward: investors aren’t necessarily abandoning technology, but they appear to be becoming more selective about which parts of it they want to own. The distinction between companies that generate capital and companies that constantly need to raise it is becoming increasingly important.

I was also interested to hear about Citrini Research’s latest State of the Themes report, covered this morning by Dow Jones’ MarketWatch. The firm is now making an argument remarkably similar to one I’ve been discussing for roughly two months, when the Nasdaq was approximately 10% higher. But that’s great. Citrini does good work, there’s plenty of room in this lifeboat and I’m happy to see some validation on my thoughts from August, when I wrote: The Real AI Crash Will Start This Year

Citrini’s central prediction is that we’re approaching peak growth in AI capital expenditures. The firm estimates that annualized hyperscaler investment is approaching $1 trillion, while annual recurring revenue across the AI ecosystem is roughly one-fifth of that amount. Those aren’t directly comparable financial measures, but the disparity highlights the fundamental question I’ve been asking: where are the returns on all this spending?

The firm argues what I have written about the last month or two…that capital markets cannot indefinitely accommodate the extraordinary financing demands of the hyperscalers and that spending growth will eventually have to decelerate. It also points to growing pricing competition between OpenAI and Anthropic, the potential commoditization of AI models, and the increasing risk that AI disrupts established software businesses without necessarily producing attractive returns for the companies building it. It’s Official: The AI Emperor Has No Clothes

This among other things, was also covered in an article I published in August reviewing 8 different bear cases facing the market by 8 well known respected investors: 8 Sharp Bear Cases You Must Read Today

Add the election’s potential implications for data-center permitting, energy infrastructure, and regulatory oversight, and the investment case becomes even more complicated.

Perhaps most interestingly, Citrini is also shifting attention toward relative value and overlooked parts of the real economy, including consumer businesses, traditional software, financials, entertainment, and energy. Its report highlights companies like Victoria’s Secret, e.l.f. Beauty, IMAX, Cinemark, and MGM Resorts, alongside relative-value trades within technology. I like their take a lot. Hopefully, we’re both right.

Their take fits with my broader expectation that the next phase of the market may favor established businesses over speculative promises. It doesn’t mean AI disappears or that every technology stock declines. It means the days of indiscriminately rewarding anything associated with AI may be ending.

Overnight trading in Asia also reflected that possibility. South Korea’s Kospi fell roughly 5%, with semiconductor names like Samsung and SK Hynix under significant pressure, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 3.6% as Tencent and Alibaba rallied more than 6%.

One session doesn’t establish a trend, but taken alongside JPMorgan’s observations and this morning’s Dow/Nasdaq divergence, the evidence of a potential rotation is becoming more interesting.

There’s another possible explanation for some of yesterday’s relative strength in large technology companies and data-center names like Microsoft. As I discussed yesterday, Elon Musk and his businesses could become particularly prominent targets for scrutiny under the new political environment.

If congressional attention initially concentrates on Tesla, SpaceX, Starlink, and Musk’s relationships with the federal government, other technology companies could enjoy some relative relief simply because investors perceive them as less immediately exposed. That’s speculative, but plausible, and it doesn’t mean the broader AI industry is out of the woods.

In fact, I expect news flow surrounding Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX to be directionally negative for a while. Questions involving autonomous driving, government contracts, environmental permitting, subsidies, and political relationships could all attract greater attention. That doesn’t imply wrongdoing or guarantee enforcement action, but it introduces uncertainty into businesses whose valuations already reflect enormous expectations.

I also want to emphasize another risk I didn’t spend enough time discussing yesterday: prediction markets.

I think these platforms could come under serious congressional and regulatory scrutiny, particularly around the distinction between financial instruments and gambling, potential market manipulation, insider information, and contracts tied to political events.

Robinhood (HOOD) is the most obvious publicly traded name I associate with this exposure, although other public companies have interests in the broader ecosystem. Prediction markets generated $433 million in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, compared with just $40 million in the comparable 2025 period. That makes them one of Robinhood's most important growth engines

Prediction markets aren’t necessarily going away, but I suspect investors may be underestimating the political and regulatory risks associated with their rapid expansion.

I also wanted to, again, reiterate the sector postives and negatives I see from the election that I laid out yesterday. Here’s what sectors I think will face headwinds, and others I think will benefit from yesterday’s election outcome.

My outlook remains essentially unchanged…both since yesterday’s reaction, since last week’s speculation the election could crash markets, and since August when I first floated the idea of the AI crash.

I still expect technology, particularly speculative AI infrastructure, to move lower over the short to medium term. Yesterday’s rally looked to me like a significant amount of election-related hedging being unwound, not evidence that the fundamental problems facing the sector have disappeared.

At the same time, I think we’re beginning to see evidence of the rotation I’ve been anticipating for 2027. JPMorgan’s trading desk is observing demand for large-cap quality and more selective technology exposure. Citrini is now advocating a shift toward relative value and overlooked real-economy businesses. And this morning, Dow futures are outperforming Nasdaq futures, widening the spread between the two from the last month…

None of that guarantees the rotation will persist. A meaningful decline in interest rates, stronger-than-expected earnings, or convincing evidence of attractive returns on AI spending could change the outlook. And established large-cap businesses aren’t automatically cheap or immune to a broader market decline.

But the combination of stretched valuations, enormous capital requirements, sticky inflation, potentially higher-for-longer interest rates, and a more complicated political environment continues to make me cautious.

I don’t think the next phase of this market will necessarily be about abandoning equities altogether. I think it will be about abandoning the assumption that every speculative growth story deserves an extraordinary valuation.

I’ve been making that argument for two months, since the Nasdaq was roughly 10% higher. It’s encouraging to see more institutional commentary moving in the same direction, but I suspect the adjustment still has further to run.

The rally hasn’t changed my mind. If anything, the emerging rotation is making the underlying thesis more compelling. God bless and have a great Thursday.

items.title: How The Historic Blue Tsunami Could End In Tears For Democrats
items.content_text:
How The Historic Blue Tsunami Could End In Tears For Democrats

Democrats are celebrating one of their biggest midterm victories in decades, but their historic triumph could come with a nasty political hangover.

The party's sweeping gains in Tuesday's elections delivered a major rebuke to President Donald Trump, as voter frustration over the Iran war, soaring gas prices and the cost of living fueled a nationwide Democratic surge.

However, the New York Post's Isaac Schorr argued in an op-ed that Democrats' biggest victory could quickly become their next political headache.

The problem is simple: Trump isn't going anywhere.

Schorr argues that even with Congress under Democratic control, Trump's veto power could prevent the party from delivering on its legislative agenda:

"With President Donald Trump in the White House and his veto pen in hand, they won't be able to push through any of their major agenda items"

However, there is another problem, according to Schorr:

"His caucus won't let him work with Trump during his waning days in the White House"

Schorr suggests Democrats could negotiate deals on energy production, immigration enforcement and government spending. Instead, the columnist predicts the party will prioritize confrontation:

"Alas, instead it'll be all talk and no work on behalf of their constituents."

Schorr also warned that Democrats could revive divisive battles over immigration, spending, climate policy and transgender participation in women's sports, while potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump.

Schorr closed with a warning that could prove prescient:

"But they're equally likely to give themselves a years-long hangover - by reminding Americans of who they really are."

Republicans suffered a string of major Senate defeats in states long considered Republican strongholds. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico toppled Ken Paxton, while Adam Hamilton ousted Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas. Moreover, the biggest shock came in South Carolina, where Annie Andrews defeated Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the late Lindsey Graham.

Democrats also flipped House districts across the country, securing control of both chambers of Congress.

LAWYER UP.

— Congressman Robert Garcia (@RepRobertGarcia) November 4, 2026

Yet, in surprising twist that could complicate Schorr's argument, Trump revealed last night that he has already spoke with Democrat leaders and expressed a willingness to work together.

"Well, we're going to work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country. Very important. They've already called and they want to work with," Trump told POLITICO's Dasha Burns. "[I] have the right to veto everything, but I don't want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything. They want to see things happen, too."

However, Democrats now have the power to investigate the Trump administration and block legislation, and they're already talking tough. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA) wasted no time sending Trump and his Republican allies a blunt two-word warning: "Lawyer up."

items.title: "Neither Does It Seem To Be The Last": Bank Of England Hikes For First Time Since 2023, Sees Inflation Near 5%
items.content_text:
"Neither Does It Seem To Be The Last": Bank Of England Hikes For First Time Since 2023, Sees Inflation Near 5%

For the first time in 1,190 days, the Bank of England has raised interest rates.

On Thursday the BoE's Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 to lift Bank Rate by 25bps to 4.00%, the first hike since August 3, 2023, when the BoE topped out at 5.25%. And the lone dissenter was no dove: external member Catherine Mann wanted a half-point move to 4.25%. Put differently, not a single one of the nine MPC members voted to keep rates on hold, which is a little more hawkish than consensus: Goldman and JPMorgan both expected a 7-2 vote (Goldman's STIR desk had Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor as the holdouts), while Deutsche Bank's UK economists were looking for a 6-3 split.

Even the doves came along, if grudgingly. Alan Taylor, one of the most dovish members of the committee, called it "a risk management, 'one-for-now' insurance hike," while Governor Andrew Bailey, in his own written paragraph, went a step further:

"I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach... Today's increase shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes. But, unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem to be the last increase."

In other words, December is live, and traders took the hint: according to Bloomberg, the market now prices roughly a 50% chance of another quarter-point hike next month, and almost three more 25bp hikes by the end of 2027. Two-year gilt yields rose 3bps to 4.77%, and the pound steadied around $1.3472.

Regular readers won't be surprised. Back in March, just weeks into the Iran war, a 9-0 "hawkish hold" sent UK gilt yields exploding higher on a surprise BoE rate-hike threat, with 2Y yields jumping 30bps in a day. And in September, when the BoE held at 3.75% in a 6-3 vote (Mann, Huw Pill and Megan Greene already voting to hike), we warned that the decision would "leave a near-term hike firmly in play," so we'll allow ourselves a modest victory lap.

With today's move, the BoE joins a club that is getting crowded: the Fed hiked for the first time since July 2023 back in September, the RBA has been hiking into a housing slump, and with Euro area headline inflation at a 3-year high of 4.0%, the ECB probably isn't far behind. Which, as Goldman put it last weekend, makes central banks the market's last "source of calm"... "good luck."

From 3.2% To 4.9% In One Report

The reason for the hawkish turn is in the BoE's new November Monetary Policy Report. CPI inflation, which was 3.5% in September, is now projected to peak at 4.9% in Q2 2027, the highest since September 2023. Just three months ago, in the July forecasts, the BoE saw inflation peaking at a much more benign 3.2%. That's quite a revision for one quarter, even by central bank forecasting standards.

Most of the overshoot is mechanical: household utility bills and motor fuel accounted for around 60% of September's overshoot of the 2% target, and it's about to get worse. The Ofgem price cap is expected to rise to around £2,150 in Q1 2027 from £1,723 in Q4, a ~25% jump in household energy bills in January, with another increase likely in April. Direct energy effects alone are projected to add around 1.4 percentage points to CPI in Q1.

The BoE admits there is "limited evidence" so far of second-round effects in wages and prices, but it suspects that is a timing issue: firms have been shielded by "hedging and long-term fixed price contracts," and the MPC fears pass-through will come once those expire. And the scenarios are not pretty. In the adverse case of repeated escalations in the Iran conflict, CPI hits 6.2% in Q3 2027; in the "weaker demand" scenario, inflation instead collapses to 1.2%, which would, ironically, require rate cuts.

Meanwhile the economy has been more resilient than the BoE expected (or maybe just more resilient than it wanted): the 2026 GDP forecast was upgraded to 1.6% from 1.1%, and 2027 to 1.3% from 1.1%, although 2028 was cut to 1.2% from 1.7% on the assumption that the energy shock lingers. The MPC's verdict: while "policy was still restrictive" before Thursday's hike, "it was less clear that this would impart sufficiently disinflationary pressure to bring inflation back to target in a timely manner."

Bailey had been laying the groundwork for weeks. Here was the Governor a month ago:

Hiking Into An Oil Crash

There is just one small problem with the BoE's inflation math: the oil price it's built on no longer exists.

The MPR's projections are conditioned on energy futures averaged over the 15 working days to October 27, during which front-month Brent averaged $108 per barrel, around 70% above pre-war levels, while UK gas futures over the forecast horizon were some 120% above their pre-conflict levels.

Then the US midterms happened. As we detailed yesterday, crude crashed as the "Blue-nami" sparked market chaos, with Brent plunging 8.7% on Wednesday to close at $94.62, beneath $100 for the first time since September, after Vance boldly admitted that "the reason we lost is the war." Physical markets were already flashing the same signal, flipping from bidding war to fire sale as Gulf barrels flood back.

That's roughly 12% below the oil price the BoE plugged into its forecast (napkin math, and Brent is a moving target). Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid noted in his Early Morning Reid that the oil slide "significantly dampen[ed] fears over inflation," and the market agreed: the Euro 1-year inflation swap plunged 25.9bps on the day to a two-month low of 3.10%.

JPMorgan's Federico Manicardi was even more explicit in his morning briefing (available to pro subs), writing that the market reads the Democratic sweep as a "flatter geopolitical risk curve on Iran," and that "lower Brent/Gas risk premia with the global oil balance already back in surplus (+1.4 mbd in October vs ~+1.3 mbd on avg last year) should ease pressure on central banks."

Good news for UK households, maybe. Less so for the credibility of a forecast that was stale before it was even published. To be fair to the BoE, the MPR itself warns that inventories are thin, European gas storage is below average and a cold winter could send prices spiking again. And Iran just rejected the latest draft proposal to end the war, so nobody should be declaring the energy shock over just yet.

Goldman: One More In February, But The Market Is Getting Ahead Of Itself

So where does Bank Rate go from here? Going into the meeting, Goldman's European economists led by Sven Jari Stehn had already pencilled in a second hike, writing in their BoE preview, "A Hike with Noncommittal Guidance" (available to pro subs), that they "now expect a second Bank Rate hike to 4.25% in February given continued upward pressure on energy prices and the stronger recent activity and labour market figures." But there is a big caveat:

"We continue to think that market pricing for over 100bp of tightening over the next year looks too high given that second-round effects into wages look contained and consumer spending growth is likely to slow over the winter."

Goldman's STIR trader Daryl Li was even blunter in this morning's GS Morning note from Adam Crook (available to pro subs). With the December, February and March meetings pricing a cumulative 36bps (down from 41bps the day before), he thinks "this pricing has more to come out with or without de-escalation, mainly because the data has been good but not exponential - we should be pricing between 0-1 hikes per quarter, not 1-2." His take on December:

"With the war still unresolved, receiving it is a short vol trade and probably can only get down to a 4bps minimum. It feels like the right trade and we need a re-escalation, with gas pushing towards 120+, before Dec MPC is truly on the table."

Well, after Bailey's "neither does it seem to be the last" line, December pricing went the other way, to roughly a coin flip. Goldman FX salesman Matt Atherton had flagged exactly this risk in his FX Morning Update (also available to pro subs), writing that the desk saw "a greater risk of an 8-1 vote rather than a tighter call," and that the key tell would be in the individual paragraphs: "greater emphasis on risks points to a December hike while greater emphasis on evidence points to more gradual hiking." Bailey's paragraph leaned a lot more toward risks than evidence.

Here's the thing though: the BoE's own staff sort of agree with Goldman. The MPR's illustrative policy paths, which the BoE stresses do not "translate mechanically" into decisions, show that the central projection requires a restrictive stance, but that "a somewhat looser policy stance than implied by the market curve is appropriate on average." In fact, the BoE's own projections, which assume Bank Rate peaks somewhere in the 4.75% to 5% range, get CPI below the 2% target by 2029, implying just one or two more hikes are needed.

One-For-Now... Or The Start Of A Hiking Cycle Nobody Wants?

That leaves the BoE with a familiar dilemma. Hike too little, and the 2022 nightmare repeats, when an energy and food shock bled into wages and services prices and kept inflation above target far longer than the Bank expected (the MPR itself warns that five years of high inflation may have made firms and workers quicker to raise prices and demand higher pay this time around). Hike too much, and the MPC is tightening into a supply shock just as UK households absorb a 25% jump in energy bills, with the "weaker demand" scenario showing inflation crashing to 1.2%. We asked back in March whether an oil supply shock really warrants central bank hikes; eight months later, the BoE has decided it does, just as oil is collapsing.

Our take: Taylor's "one-for-now" label is probably closer to the truth than the market's three-more-hikes path. If Brent holds below $100 and the Middle East keeps de-escalating, the BoE's 4.9% peak will be revised down by February, and the second-round effects the MPC is insuring against may never show up in the size it fears. If, on the other hand, Iran re-escalates and gas heads to 120+, then Goldman's trader is right that December is truly on the table, and the BoE will look prescient for hiking before the second shock rather than after it.

Either way, Bailey has managed something quite impressive: hiking rates the day after Brent crashed below $100. Then again, after showing up famously late to the 2021-22 inflation party, maybe the BoE just decided that being early is the lesser evil.

Much more in the full Goldman BoE preview, "A Hike with Noncommittal Guidance," and the "GS Morning" note, both available to pro subs.

items.title: Truist Slaps Nike With Sell Rating As Jordan Franchise Implodes
items.content_text:
Truist Slaps Nike With Sell Rating As Jordan Franchise Implodes

Nike's rally from roughly $34 a share in October to above $40 by midweek has done little to ease Wall Street analysts' skepticism about its turnaround strategy.

Earlier this week, UBS analyst Pilar Rocafort told clients, "It's still not time to buy Nike." Truist Securities reinforced Rocafort's caution on the stock in a note Thursday morning, downgrading the shares to Sell from Hold, citing "risks across the portfolio" and "an inflated valuation."

"NKE shares are up 19% over the past ~month (vs S&P flat), which we believe reflects positive sector rotations rather than an improvement in underlying fundamentals," Truist Securities retail analyst Joseph Civello wrote in a note.

Civello maintained a $29 price target and warned that fading Jordan demand, deepening weakness in China, and mounting competition threaten an already expensive stock.

How expensive is Nike at around $40 a share? 

Well, Civello said its valuation is currently around 27 times second-year forward earnings, compared with about 15 times for peers. He said prices look cheap after the multi-year bear market, but anyone buying the stock today is paying a steep premium for a turnaround whose timeline keeps slipping.

The Jordan franchise is a key problem, the analyst continued: 

For example, initial commentary on deliberate product pullbacks centered much more heavily on 3 classic franchises (AJ1, AF1 & Dunks) but has spread much more deeply & broadly across Sportswear and Jordan (60%+ of the overall business). We believe that hyped retro launches like the "Royal" AJ1, Jordan 14 Forest Green, and the Air Jordan 6 "White Infrared" (launching on 11/7), with five of seven recent Nike/Jordan launches all selling below retail, suggest meaningful brand pressure.

On top of this all, the analyst warned that the downturn in the Chinese market has yet to conclude:

We think visibility into where/when China bottoms is very limited – Despite recently becoming CFO on 8/17, Dave Denton materially slashed the China outlook, characterizing prior internal expectations as overly optimistic. Guidance now calls for the region to get worse through the year (vs F1Q's 26% CC declines) with the digital cleanup expected to take “multiple seasons.” 

In our view, mgmt's historical optimism that trends in the country would eventually improve led to them getting complacent in the region, which when combined with broadly stale innovation/marketing has driven meaningful pressure on brand equity. We struggle to identify a clear catalyst path for reaccelerating demand in the region in the NT/MT, especially as competition from local & other western brands continues to get more intense.

To sum up the note, these mounting pressures suggest Nike's latest rally has outpaced its underlying recovery. Civello maintained his $29 price target, signaling the turnaround timeline could be longer than expected.

items.title: 'Low Hire, Low Fire, Low Inspire': Claims Hit 57 Year Lows, Sentiment Still Sucks, And Payrolls Are Next
items.content_text:
'Low Hire, Low Fire, Low Inspire': Claims Hit 57 Year Lows, Sentiment Still Sucks, And Payrolls Are Next

Another week, another print showing that American employers still refuse to fire anyone in any meaningful numbers. 

Initial jobless claims remain parked near multi-decade lows, plunging to 189k this week (after recent weeks in the mid-to-high 190,000s), confirming that the 'low fire' half of the current labor market is intact.  Last week's print is officially the lowest since 1969...

And Continuing claims are holding around 1.7 million Americans...

Layoffs simply are not happening at scale.

That is the good news, such as it is.

The less comforting half is the 'low hire' reality that has now persisted for roughly three years. September JOLTS showed openings rebounding to 7.52 million and the openings rate at 4.5 percent, yet the hires rate stayed stuck at 3.4 percent with roughly 5.4 million hires. Net payroll growth has averaged in the low-to-mid tens of thousands for most of 2026. Companies are holding onto the workers they already have, posting some vacancies, and then mostly not filling them. Churn is low, mobility is limited, and the labor market has lost the dynamism that used to define expansions.

Which brings us to the 'low inspire' part that the hard data refuse to capture. University of Michigan sentiment closed October at 48.0 - flat, still near historical lows, and dominated by purchasing-power complaints, elevated inflation expectations (year-ahead ~4.7 percent), and a sense that higher rates and sticky prices have permanently eroded real incomes. The Conference Board’s confidence index managed a rebound to 91.7 in October on the back of cheaper gasoline and better present-situation readings, but the expectations component remains soft (72.6) and well below the levels that historically signaled healthy forward momentum. People still have jobs. They just do not feel particularly good about any of it.

This is the strange equilibrium the economy has settled into: resilient enough that mass layoffs have not materialized and recession odds from the employment side stay contained, yet weak enough on hiring and confidence that there is little acceleration. It is a labor market that supports the soft-landing narrative on paper while delivering almost none of the broad-based enthusiasm or wage-and-spending vigor that used to accompany 'full employment.'

Tomorrow's payrolls report will be read against exactly this backdrop. A number in the 50–80k range (or even a modest upside surprise) will be spun as 'resilient' and consistent with the low-fire claims data. A soft print will be explained away as noise or as further evidence of the low-hire regime rather than the start of something worse. 

Either way, the deeper tension remains: hard data keep saying the floor is still solid, soft data keep saying almost no one is inspired by the view from that floor. Markets will trade the headline. 

The real story is the one that has not changed in months - low hire, low fire, and still very little inspire.

items.title: Hakeem Jeffries Claims Impeachment And Getting Even With Trump Aren't Priorities
items.content_text:
Hakeem Jeffries Claims Impeachment And Getting Even With Trump Aren't Priorities

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) told reporters Wednesday morning after Democrats swept the midterms and won majorities in the House and Senate that no House Democrat has raised the subject of impeaching President Donald Trump with him.

"I haven't had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment," Jeffries claimed. "We've been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability because the House is a separate and co-equal branch of government."

.@RepJeffries: "I haven't had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment...I have not heard from President Trump." pic.twitter.com/umZspxCyhN

— CSPAN (@cspan) November 4, 2026

Jeffries, who is expected to be elected House Speaker in the next session of Congress, said impeaching Trump does not rank among his priorities, even though he used "accountability" in the same statement along with "affordability."

Despite the contradiction, he made the same case during an appearance on MSNOW's Morning Joe, where he outlined his agenda for the incoming House.

"The American people don't want us to get even," Jeffries claimed on Morning Joe. "They want us to get things done on their behalf because life is way too expensive. We ran on affordability. We won on affordability. And now it's our job to govern on affordability."

Jeffries insisted Democrats had campaigned on lowering prices for groceries, gas, housing, and health care.

"As a matter of fact, we made clear that we're fighting for an affordable America and explicitly promised the American people that we would fight hard to lower the high costs of groceries and gas and housing, and that we were gonna fight hard to make sure that healthcare was affordable for every single American, and that hardworking American taxpayers who are working hard and playing by the rules, they should be able to live an affordable life," he said. "That's our mission, that's our responsibility, and we're gonna work hard to make that happen."

Hakeem Jeffries on Morning Joe: The American people don't want us to get even. They want us to get things done on their behalf because life is way too expensive.

We ran on affordability, we won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability. pic.twitter.com/b5ieQUbMRO

— Clipping Wings (@ClippingWings) November 4, 2026

However, there's reason to be skeptical of his claims. When asked about impeachment before the election, Jeffries said Democrats "haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out." Other Democrats have spent months pledging a wave of investigations once the party regained power, and several have said Trump already meets the threshold for removal. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD) has repeatedly claimed Trump has committed numerous impeachable offenses during his second term.

Democrat Jamie Raskin - instead of working for Americans - wants to impeach President Trump but can't name an offense.

NBC: Do you believe Trump has committed impeachable offenses?

RASKIN: "Undoubtedly...we don't have time to remotely scratch the surface." pic.twitter.com/sgwJu3T42i

— RNC Research (@RNCResearch) September 6, 2026

Raskin led the second impeachment of Trump in 2021, after the January 6 Capitol riot. The Senate acquitted Trump in that trial, as it did in the first impeachment in 2020.

Further undermining Jeffries' claim that Democrats aren't interested in impeachment or revenge, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), the incoming chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, released a statement after the party secured its majority, vowing to "take on the Trump Crime Family, corporate corruption, DHS and ICE abuses, and the cover-up of the Epstein files."

Official statement from incoming chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Government Reform @RepRobertGarcia: pic.twitter.com/A4MDkPTjzq

— Oversight Dems (@OversightDems) November 4, 2026

Pressure for investigations is also coming from the party's progressive wing. Fox News reported Wednesday evening that many progressives want Democrats, who will hold majorities in both the House and the Senate, to open investigations into Trump, his family and administration officials.

Progressive commentator Brian Tyler Cohen described what he hears from his audience in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"As content creators, we hear from huge, diverse audiences, and they all want the same thing: a government that works for them: lower costs, leaders who listen, and accountability when people abuse their power," Cohen said. "Delivering results and pursuing accountability go hand in hand, provided investigations follow the evidence and serve the public."

"Creators helped people get involved in this election, and we're going to keep those conversations going, helping audiences stay informed and judge whether their elected leaders are delivering," Cohen added.

People close to the president expect a third impeachment attempt. A Trump confidant told Axios last month that a Democratic investigative push would produce a confrontation between the two sides.

"If Democrats win and start the investigations, he'll get more defiant ... Democrats won't be able to resist impeachment and he won't be able to resist daring them to do it. You think you control Donald Trump? Well, f**k you. You don't," the confidant said.

The White House said Trump remains open to working with the new majority and criticized the prospect of investigations into his administration.

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

A White House official separately pointed to the administration's federal authority as Democrats prepare to use investigations and subpoenas.

"If crazed Democrats want to abuse their power and politicize their process of investigations, subpoenas, and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers," the official said.

***

Futures Split As Blue-Wave Chip Purge Enters Day Two; Oil Rebounds, BoE Hikes

US futures are mixed, with the Nasdaq lagging as the post-midterm rotation out of chipmakers and the AI complex enters a second day, after the Democratic sweep raised fears of a data center backlash, Qualcomm tumbled on a weak forecast and the Kospi crashed almost 6%, while oil rebounded modestly from Wednesday's plunge and the BoE hiked rates for the first time in three years; as a result the 10Y yield touched 4.83%, the lowest since Sept. 10.
