Democrat Kathy Castor held onto her seat in Florida’s 14th congressional district, fending off a challenge from Republican Mike Beltran. Republicans purposefully redrew that district to get rid of Castor, by including a lot less of Tampa and a lot more of its outlying rural counties. In 2024, President Donald Trump won the areas making up this new district by 11 points.

In Florida’s 22nd congressional district, Democrat Pia Dandiya defeated Republican Casey Askar, after Governor Ron DeSantis’s gerrymandering efforts created an open seat for the Republicans to steal. The state’s current 22nd district is represented by Democrat Lois Frankel, who is now running in its 23rd district.

In the race for Florida’s Senate seat, Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist, was defeated by Republican incumbent Ashley Moody—but when the race was called at 84.3 percent of the vote reported, Moody led Nixon by only 0.7 percentage points. The Republican won, but not by nearly as much as expected for a historically red state.

items.title: Democrats Take Control of the House of Representatives
items.content_text:
Democrats are projected to retake control of the House of Representatives for the first time in four years.

Decision Desk HQ projected Democrats will seize the chamber from Republicans. It is not yet clear which party has taken control of the Senate.

Republicans gained control of the House two years ago during the 2022 midterm elections. While there was no “red wave” as widely predicted, Republicans were able to flip 19 districts from blue to red.

Ahead of the midterm elections Tuesday, Republicans held only a slim four-seat majority over Democrats. The latest polls had heavily indicated that Democrats would retake control of the House.

While America’s authoritarian era likely won’t end in a day, the results of the House midterm elections are a searing indictment on Republicans’ rule and the first two years of Trump’s second term.

items.title: Leaked Texts Expose GOP in Key Swing State Bracing for Disaster
items.content_text:
Midterm election predictions are not looking good for Republicans in battleground states.

Garrett Archer, a data analyst for an Arizona ABC News affiliate, shared messages Tuesday from an unnamed GOP analyst that don’t bode well for their party.

“God all my models are already projecting doom. And it’s 8am,” the text messages read.

Conservative campaigns around the country are feeling similar pressure as their candidates were forced to thread the needle between kowtowing to the president’s fragile ego and distancing themselves from his wildly unpopular military and economic policies.

Politico reported Friday that some Republicans are bracing for “a brutal evening,” expecting major losses in both chambers of Congress.

“Once the dominoes start falling it becomes hard to stop them,” a senior GOP strategist told the newsroom.

Donald Trump has already started surveying the landscape of his Cabinet for potential fall guys should the elections go south. Last month, Trump reportedly called several close confidants to assess the job performance of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, his former campaign manager and famed “Ice Maiden,” as a potential scapegoat for a major midterm bust. He’s also made the rounds to assess current attitudes about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine as the Iran war drags on into its eighth month.

Republicans, meanwhile, know exactly where to point their fingers.

“We all know who the problem is. It’s Trump,” a GOP strategist involved in midterm races across the country told Politico Monday.

That same strategist was unsure about how the Republican Party might reform itself if the party sustains major losses on Tuesday.

“Look, a lot of Republicans have held their tongues. A lot of Republicans who have real problems with the way things have gone the last two years have been good soldiers,” they said. “But what happens if we lose 35 House seats and six Senate seats?”

items.title: Trump DOJ Targets Democrats in Senate Race Probe Right Before Election
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump is taking drastic steps to investigate Alaska’s Senate election, with the Department of Justice sending criminal target letters to about 20 leading Democrats.

The New York Times reported on Election Day that Marc Elias, a Democratic elections lawyer whose firm represents Alaska Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola, has received a letter. So has at least one official at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. The letters tell the recipients that they could be targets in the DOJ’s investigation into the recruitment of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.

The DOJ is investigating possible donor fraud and conspiracy charges as well, an anonymous source told the Times. According to the publication, it’s not known when the letters were sent or if every intended recipient got them.

Trump has been raving about the Alaska contest for days, accusing the Democratic Party of election fraud and repeatedly attacking Elias and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. Trump told Fox & Friends Tuesday morning that Elias “was a bad guy, very bad guy” who “should go to jail, in my opinion.”

On Monday night, Trump made a series of Truth Social posts claiming that independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan was “missing in action” and suggesting that he had been kidnapped. He speculated that “the Dumocrats are trying to steal this Race by putting a FAKE Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr. on the Ballot. People will not be able to figure it out, and many Votes will be lost.”

That, along with the target letters, could be a hint that Trump will try to take action in the event that Peltola wins the race. He’s openly said that he would consider a “redo” of the election if that happens, although he lacks the legal backing to make such a move, especially considering Alaska has ranked-choice voting. He’d end up sowing confusion and undermining confidence not just in Alaska, but in the entire country.

items.title: Google Tries to Blackmail Schools Into Using Its AI Tools
items.content_text:
Schools that reject Google’s AI services apparently won’t be allowed to use Google at all.

The company announced Tuesday that it will turn off search engine access for K-12 schools that toggle off its AI tools as soon as next year. Google executives claim the decision is based on the technologies’ recent fusion.

“Search and AI are deeply integrated,” Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times, adding that students at schools that have banned AI “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Many schools across the country have already invested in Google’s technologies, purchasing low-cost Google Chromebooks to assist educational instruction. Beyond that, Google’s search algorithm has led the industry for the last two decades, besting its competitors to the point that its mere name has become synonymous with research.

Lina Khan, the former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, argued in a statement on X that Google had used its “search monopoly to coerce schools” into adopting AI tools. She noted Google has been found legally liable multiple times for antitrust law violations.

“This latest move shows it remains unchastened,” Khan wrote. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools … Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

Studies conducted over the last several months have indicated that the risks attached to the use of AI in schools outweigh the potential benefits. A January report by the Brookings Institution’s Center for Universal Education found that AI can “undermine children’s foundational development,” and that “the damages it has already caused are daunting.”

New skill development and problem-solving abilities are among the chief concerns when it comes to early-age AI dependence. Children can easily fall into a catch-22 in which they continually offload their work onto the AI, diminishing their self-confidence and self-reliance in the process, according to the Brookings Institution report.

“When kids use generative AI that tells them what the answer is,” Rebecca Winthrop, one of the report’s authors, told NPR, “they are not thinking for themselves. They’re not learning to parse truth from fiction. They’re not learning to understand what makes a good argument. They’re not learning about different perspectives in the world because they’re actually not engaging in the material.”

items.title: Trump Team Tries to Claim High Prices Are Good, Right Before Election
items.content_text:
The Trump administration’s final pitch to voters on Election Day seems to be that higher prices are a good thing.

Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins told Newsmax Tuesday afternoon that the United States was “going to have record exports this year for corn and wheat and cotton and other incredible American industries while those prices are rising. So we’ve made so much progress.”

Rollins’s prediction that exports are going to go up while prices also rise seems to be rather presumptive, as people tend to buy less of a product when prices are high. And corn exports are actually down this year compared to previous years.

Rollins wasn’t the only administration official touting high prices as a positive. Energy Secretary Chris Wright went on Fox Business Tuesday morning saying, “This is what capitalism is all about.

“The markets are sending that price mechanism right now. Prices are high. The best cure for high prices is high prices. It grows supply,” Wright said.

Wright didn’t mention that high prices grow supply because fewer products are being purchased, which isn’t good for businesses or the economy. The American consumer is finding it harder to make ends meet, and at the end of the day, their disposable income doesn’t go as far. Consumer confidence has massively declined this year thanks to the Iran war and the president’s whimsical tariffs, and people are going to make that known in the voting booth.

items.title: Key Swing States Say DOJ’s “Election Monitors” Are Acting Out
items.content_text:
For the first time in U.S. history, the White House is monitoring elections across the entire country—and they’ve already crossed the line.

The Justice Department announced Tuesday that it had placed roughly 1,000 election monitors and observers in all 50 states. They will be assessing polling places for compliance with federal election statutes.

The declaration also specified more than 100 jurisdictions that the agency intends to monitor. Most of the inclusions are either Democratic strongholds or hotly contested districts in the midterm elections.

“Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division,” Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet K. Dhillon said in a statement. “I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.”

Previous administrations have similarly tapped monitors to oversee election cycles, but never before at this level. In 2024, the DOJ monitored 86 jurisdictions across 27 states. It was the largest such effort by the DOJ since at least 2004. But some election officials have already flagged the 2026 rollout as a potential intimidation tactic that could scare voters away from actually participating at the ballot box.

Within hours of the DOJ announcement, New Mexico’s secretary of state told PBS NewsHour that some of the agency’s monitors had been asking “some unusual questions and doing things that are not allowed by law such as questioning voters” in Bernalillo County.

A spokesperson for the Justice Department subsequently told NewsHour that their “team had a productive call with the New Mexico Secretary of State just a few minutes ago,” and that they “believe the issue is resolved and will not affect our ongoing monitoring for the rest of the day.”

Similar complaints also emerged out of Michigan. There were at least two instances in Dearborn and Flint in which the DOJ’s election monitors overstepped their authority, a spokesperson for the Michigan Attorney General’s Office told the Detroit Free Press. The monitors reportedly asked election workers for copies of their training materials and the training they personally received.

DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels told VoteBeat that the monitors “asked their typical questions about election official training.”

“These are standard questions on the forms we provided our monitors. They are the same questions asked by monitors in the past, including during the previous administration,” Pels said.

Since 2020, Donald Trump and his allies have relentlessly opined about alleged voter fraud, attempting to not only rewrite prior election results but also unravel the tools of future elections, such as mail-in voting. But his rhetoric has also had the auxiliary effect of damaging public trust in American democracy, disenfranchising voters—and their faith in their individual power—as a result.

Dhillon herself has been tied to prominent election deniers and conspiracy theorists, including the president, 2022 Arizona gubernatorial candidate Kari Lake, and former Trump fixer Rudy Giuliani.

Earlier this year, Dhillon oversaw a series of lawsuits against dozens of state election officials as the administration attempted to gain access to local voter rolls containing sensitive information, such as Social Security numbers, as part of a nationwide investigation to uncover noncitizens who might vote in the November election.

One arm of that legal effort was torn to shreds by a judge last week, who argued that “never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”

This story has been updated.

items.title: Jan 6er Pardoned by Trump Charged for Threatening to Execute Judges
items.content_text:
A man pardoned by President Donald Trump after making threats in Washington, D.C., after the January 6 Capitol riot was just charged for making threats against federal judges.

Cleveland Grover Meredith Jr. made multiple social media posts over the past few years, including commentary related to January 6, supporting Trump, and expressing QAnon conspiracy theories. At least one of them caught the attention of federal agents, according to a recent court filing.

In an April post on Facebook, Meredith said, “ALL J6 Federal JUDGES will be executed” with grinning and middle-finger emojis. In another post, Meredith threatened 10 federal judges by name, warning that “[Pete] Hegseth has plans 4U.”

Meredith’s posts have drawn attention from federal agents before, with the FBI interviewing him on November 12, 2024, and August 14, 2025. His April post, however, crossed the line, according to FBI Special Agent Richard Taylor, who said in a criminal complaint that due to Meredith’s history of “violent online rhetoric,” his post was either for “(i) the purpose of issuing a threat, (ii) with knowledge that his post would be viewed as a threat, or (iii) while consciously disregarding a substantial risk that his post would be viewed as a threat.”

This criminal complaint is very similar to the charges that Meredith faced in 2021. While he arrived in Washington too late to take part in the Capitol insurrection thanks to car trouble, he sent a text message from a hotel room to a relative the next day allegedly threatening to “put a bullet” in then–House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s head.

The FBI arrested Meredith, and after he consented to a search of his hotel room, they “found a 9 mm semi-automatic firearm, an assault-style rifle with a telescopic sight, approximately 2,500 rounds of ammunition, and multiple large-capacity ammunition feeding devices inside the trailer.” Meredith pleaded guilty to interstate communication of threats and was sentenced to 28 months in prison, though he later was included in Trump’s mass pardons and clemency for January 6 defendants.

Now Meredith is in trouble with the law again, not unlike other Capitol insurrectionists. As of June, at least 97 of them, or about one in 16, have been arrested for various crimes, including child molestation and reckless homicide, after they were pardoned.

items.title: Haley Stevens Rocks Unfortunate Hat to Vote for Mike Rogers
items.content_text:
Representative Haley Stevens does not seem to be handling her growing rift with the Democratic Party very well.

On Tuesday morning, the Michigan Democrat indicated she was unwilling to speak with the press before diving into a nonsensical diatribe as she marched into a polling place in Birmingham, Michigan, on her mother’s arm.

“Does it feel worth it to have endorsed Mike Rogers today? Any comment at all?” asked NewsNation’s Hannah Brandt.

“Look, I’m with my mom, this is our tradition here. You know what this is? It’s the people’s day,” Stevens said, with her enormous Vince Camuto straw Panama hat partially shielding her face. “And I—I told this to our Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries—it’s Majority Makers Day.”

“What do you mean by that?” Brandt pressed.

“And look, I released a big article, or set of thoughts, yesterday,” Stevens said, referring to an 890-word AI-assisted plea that she published on her X account.

“That’s right, I did read that. I want to know, does it feel worth it, ma’am?” Brandt asked.

“Absolutely, voting is always worth it,” Stevens concluded.

Stevens imploded her reputation and doomed her political prospects over the weekend. On Friday, Stevens demanded that Dr. Abdul El-Sayed—the man who bested her in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary—apologize for his prior criticism of Israel. Representative Debbie Dingell then waded into the mix, disinviting Stevens from a church event with El-Sayed and Representative James E. Clyburn, one of Stevens’s lower-chamber mentors.

That’s when Stevens went berserk. Rather than attempt to make peace or let bygones be bygones, she did a complete 180 and endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, aligning herself with the MAGA endorsee in an apparent effort to undermine El-Sayed’s odds. Notably, she did so without telling anyone, as her staff was reportedly at the El-Sayed event waiting for her arrival.

Since then, even Stevens’s aides have abandoned her in favor of El-Sayed. On Monday, nearly two dozen of her former Senate campaign staffers torched her recent behavior as “selfish,” “irrational,” and “shameful” in an open letter.

“For over a year, Rep. Stevens criticized Mike Rogers as a corrupt career politician who would blindly rubber-stamp Donald Trump’s chaos, regardless of the damage it inflicted on Michiganders. It’s infuriating to watch her become the very thing she once condemned,” they wrote.

“She told CNN there was too much ‘on the line’ to play games a few days ago,” the former staffers wrote. “Now, she’s doing just that. Her appalling behavior is an insult to anyone who wasted even a moment of their time supporting her campaign.”

Stevens’s MAGA endorsement could even cost her her job, as Democrats mull calls to banish her from the House, NBC News reported on Tuesday.

items.title: Trump Makes Stunning Announcement About Aid for Israel
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump told Fox & Friends on Tuesday morning that U.S. aid to Israel will cease at the end of the year.

“We were giving them $4 billion. We are, but it gets cut off at the end of the year,” Trump said. When host Brian Kilmeade asked why, the president replied, “Because they don’t need it,” saying Israeli officials told him as much.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an [Abdul] El-Sayed when they don’t need it? It’s a bad talking point, because you say, why don’t we give everybody $4 billion? Israel’s our number one, we give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it. We’ve been doing it for years, I’ve been doing it. But Israel is a very thriving country, they don’t need it,” Trump continued, saying that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu brought up the issue with him and that they have come to an agreement.

“[Netanyahu] understands that this is one of their points of contention. Israel’s been a great ally, much more reliable than most,” Trump added, before going off on a tangent about Europe.

Trump didn’t specify whether he meant military or general aid was ending, even when Kilmeade asked him to clarify. The U.S. has sent $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel since October 2023, and efforts to cut off aid to the country due to the genocide in Gaza have failed in Congress despite support from nearly half of House Democrats.

But Trump’s pledge, even if it’s true, likely does not mean an end to U.S. support for Israel. The House passed Section 219 of the National Defense Authorization Act earlier this year integrating U.S. and Israel defense technology, which could effectively be a backdoor to more taxpayer funding for Israel’s military. Plus, Trump could easily be making an empty promise in a last-ditch election ploy.

items.title: Trump Loses His Mind Over Key Senate Race Hours Before Election
items.content_text:
Republicans appear to be on the brink of losing power in Congress—and Donald Trump is not handling it well.

The president freaked out on Monday night in a series of Truth Social posts about the Alaska Senate race, where Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is not only up against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola but also an independent candidate and retired schoolteacher sharing his name: Daniel J. Sullivan.

“FAKE ALASKA CANDIDATE DANIAL J. SULLIVAN, JR., IS MISSING IN ACTION!” Trump wrote online at 1:12 a.m. “HE HAS TOTALLY DISAPPEARED, GONE! NOBODY HAS BEEN ABLE TO FIND HIM.”

CBS News reported on Saturday that the political independent had left his hometown and flown to Anchorage. A source that witnessed him board the plane told the network that he and his wife are locally known as “world travelers.”

Two days before that, The New York Times reported that Sullivan was recruited by individuals connected to Peltola’s campaign.

“MAYBE HE HAS BEEN ‘KIDNAPPED’ BY THE CORRUPT DUMOCRAT LAWYERS??? THEY ARE SCARED STIFF OF BEING PROSECUTED FOR ELECTION FRAUD!!!” Trump continued.

In another post, Trump urged the “GREAT PEOPLE OF ALASKA” to vote for the Republican incumbent, as well as Bernadette Wilson for governor and Nick Begich for the House.

“These Great Patriots have my Complete and Total Endorsement—They will never let you down!” Trump wrote.

In yet another post, Trump claimed that “no one has done more for Alaska than ‘TRUMP’” but that “Dan Sullivan has been with us all the way.”

“The Dumocrats are trying to steal this Race by putting a FAKE Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr. on the Ballot. People will not be able to figure it out, and many Votes will be lost,” Trump wrote.

Alaskans have already widely refuted the administration’s concerns, insisting that they’re capable of reading. One Anchorage resident told CNN last week that the controversy hasn’t shaken his vote at all, saying that you can “absolutely” tell who’s who on the ballot.

“And I don’t even have my glasses on,” he quipped. “It’s pretty clear. It’s in black and white.”

items.title: Here Are Some Ballot Measures to Watch on Tuesday
items.content_text:
You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.


Inside Washington

As votes roll in throughout Election Day, most eyes will be on the balance of the House and Senate. But in some states, voters will be directly deciding on some of the biggest political questions of the decade—including how to run a modern democracy. Ballot initiatives in some states could reduce voters’ rights and power. In others, voters have the chance to enshrine those rights and reject partisan gerrymandering.

“Amid rising authoritarianism, the fight for democracy is also happening through ballot initiatives,” said Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, the executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center. “This year, we’re seeing more attacks from politicians on voters’ rights,” agreed Hannah Ledford, the deputy executive director at the Fairness Project. “And voters are having to defend those rights at the ballot box more than ever really, in an election.”

Six states are considering voter ID rules, some of which mirror President Donald Trump’s SAVE America Act. Ohio and North Carolina already require identification at the polls, but ballot measures would put that in the states’ constitutions. Nevada, too, is trying to amend its constitution to require photo ID to vote. Arizona has a measure requiring those voting by mail-in ballot to somehow show ID. Even in blue California and Colorado, voters will consider similar measures. Experts say that voter ID laws end up suppressing the votes of Black voters, students, and Native voters, while failing to actually address election fraud (which is exceedingly rare).

In North Dakota, South Dakota, and Utah, voters will decide on measures that would make it harder to pass constitutional amendments in the future. Experts say that could remove a key source of power for voters by making it harder for them to practice direct democracy. In recent years, voters have used ballot initiatives to enact progressive policies like raising the minimum wage or protecting abortion rights—to the chagrin of conservative legislators. “Politicians that are really upset with the progress that voters have made in their backyard, trying to take direct democracy back, they are trying to make it harder to use and harder to pass things at the ballot box,” Ledford said.

Some ballot initiatives, though, give voters the opportunity to enshrine their rights. Missouri’s Amendment 6 would require 80 percent support in both legislative chambers and another statewide vote to change laws approved by voters or enact laws that voters rejected by referendum. That’s crucially important in a state where voters have approved progressive multiple ballot initiatives that the Republican legislature has then altered or outright reversed. “Voters in Missouri just two years ago passed the right to reproductive freedom at the ballot box. The legislature is trying to take it away and install a near-total abortion ban in the state, and voters are going to decide tomorrow whether or not politicians overreached,” Ledford said. Similar things have happened with paid sick leave and raising the minimum wage.

Missouri will also be voting on gerrymandering—specifically, via Proposition A, the redrawn 2025 map that the Supreme Court blocked for this election. “Voters in Missouri, it feels like we are in a battle with our elected officials to have our voices heard, and it’s really frustrating,” said Richard von Glahn, the executive director of People Not Politicians, about the gerrymandered maps. He’s hopeful that voters will reject the Republican maps and, through Amendment 6, will block Republican legislators from reconsidering the maps next year. “Missourians were so angry about seeing our elections really just rigged like this,” he said, “that we actually gathered about three times as many signatures as was needed” to get Prop A on the ballot. “Voters are really indicating that they should be the central focus of our democracy and the ultimate power brokers.”

These battles, which could shape the state of U.S. politics for years to come, will be playing out not just through voting rights and gerrymandering measures, but also through ballot initiatives that address abortion and trans rights. Fields suggests watching these initiatives to get a preview of future strategies to restrict bodily autonomy for women and LGBTQ individuals. “I do think ’26 is a testing ground,” she said, “for what conservatives may go full throttle [on] in 2028.”

—Emma Janssen


Outside Washington

Democrat Josh Turek’s race against Republican Ashley Hinson in Iowa could decide the balance of the Senate. On Monday, the Des Moines Register’s Stephen Gruber-Miller reported on the Republican National Committee’s self-described all-out attempt to sway the outcome. Among the efforts: The RNC and the Hinson campaign have executed the first “coordinated ad buy”—which a Supreme Court ruling made possible this summer—worth $5 million. It’s not the only last-ditch Republican attempt to win the state, but this one sounds a little more organized than President Donald Trump’s off-script remarks at a rally in Dubuque over the weekend, wherein he inexplicably went on a tangent about Hinson’s weight loss. The last New York Times/Siena poll had Turek up by one point, which was well within the margin of error.

Elsewhere:

On Monday, supermarket chains in multiple European countries reported that their cold storage systems had been targeted in a cyberattack overnight, with temps rising as high as 122 degrees, rendering the food unusable. A similar attack occurred in France last month, and the latest cold storage failure in Europe arrived days after Reuters reported, based on anonymous sources, that the Pentagon is treating cold storage failures that happened on military bases in August as a cyberattack, as well. It’s hard to overstate how crucial networks of cold storage facilities (known as the “cold chain”) are to both food and medicine supply chains in the present world—both domestically and for international trade.

Media outlets and experts alike were already facing a difficult balancing act on the topic of threat preparedness. But then last week, news on three separate but related fronts raised further alarms: Pete Hegseth’s “FORTRESS America” initiative instructing U.S. military bases to prepare for 90 days without grid power, former Trump FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino’s call for nationwide household prepping, and the British government’s new “Be Ready” campaign urging people to stock up on canned goods and emergency radios. Combined, those caused a fair amount of anxiety in certain circles. “The line between giving people solid, grounded, actionable information and stirring panic is incredibly fine,” Texas A&M professor Angela Clendenin told Fox Baltimore when asked about Bongino’s remarks in particular. But, properly executed, “preparedness avoids panic,” she added. Several experts, both in the Fox Baltimore piece and in a Guardian piece published on Monday, noted that the U.S. has long recommended that people keep several days’ worth of supplies on hand—and that Trump-era cuts to federal emergency management, along with everything else, have made this an even better idea. 

—Heather Souvaine Horn


The Ideas Factory

In a new report titled “Tracking the Return on Investment of Trump’s Backers,” the Center for American Progress’s Devon Ombers, Ryan Koronowski, and Will Ragland estimate that more than 75 “individuals and entities” have donated almost $1.7 billion to Trump’s pet projects, and in return, they “have reaped or will reap benefits conservatively estimated at approximately $183 billion.”

A new report from Arnav Rao at Open Markets Institute warns that robotaxis could “extend Big Tech’s monopoly power from the digital world into the physical world, putting the future of American transportation under the control of just a few, already-dominant corporations.” Instead of fixating on whether driverless cars are safe, Rao argues, policymakers should be looking at, for example, breaking up vertically integrated monopolies and ensuring that regulators have the tools that they need for this new landscape.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Four Questions For: Tim Grieve, editor in chief of The Washington Sun 

Q: Who are you, and what are you working on right now? 

A: I’m the editor in chief of The Washington Sun, the news publication formerly known as NOTUS. And here’s a sentence you won’t hear a lot in journalism: I spend most of my time hiring. We dove in when The Washington Post pulled back—expanding our coverage of political Washington and adding coverage of local news and sports. We’re the fastest-growing newsroom in D.C., and maybe the world: We started 2026 with 45 journalists. We’re at 110 today, and we’re just getting started. 

Q: The Washington Sun is launching at a time of layoffs, consolidation, and growing billionaire control of the media. What does a news organization have to do differently to build something durable in this environment? 

A: Hire the best people, be disciplined about what you do, and find a revenue model to support it. No problem, right? 

Q: Washington reporting can be a breed of its own, with its fixation on access, insiders, and the daily churn of politics. What does the D.C. press corps understand well, and where does it still have blind spots? 

A: Not surprisingly, the D.C. press corp understands … D.C. We’ll find out this week how well we understand the rest of the country. 

Q: What do people outside Washington misunderstand about the way journalism works here? 

A: Way too many people think that journalists just make stuff up. There have definitely been a few famous fabulists in journalism history. But I’ve worked in this business off and on for more than 40 years, and I can’t think of a single time one of my colleagues made up a story or fabricated a quote, a source, or a fact. Do we get things wrong sometimes? Sure. But journalists at reputable news organizations try very, very hard to get it right.

Interview by Indigo Olivier


Political Trivia Question of the Day  

You’ve undoubtedly heard over the course of the campaign that Kansas last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 1932. But how many Democrats has the state sent to the Senate in its entire history, going back to 1861? (Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: Supreme Court Hands Trump Huge Loss in Voter Suppression Scheme
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump’s attempt to mess with California’s elections has been shot down by the Supreme Court.

In a one-sentence rejection with no explanation, the court ruled on Monday evening against the Trump administration’s emergency request that California separate 20,000 ballots that the White House claims were cast by noncitizens. There do not appear to have been any dissents.

Election officials in California and Los Angeles County said that the administration’s list was unreliable, pointing to their own findings that many on the list were actually U.S.-born citizens. The Trump administration even admitted that the list contained inaccuracies but still insisted that California comply with its demands. Late last month, the DOJ sued to force California to separate those 20,000 ballots.

Last week, U.S. District Judge David Carter issued a blistering ruling castigating the White House for acting like a monarchy.

“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote at the time. “In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.”

Now the Supreme Court has affirmed Carter’s ruling and protected California’s ballots from Trump’s interference. That hasn’t stopped the Trump administration from arresting people based on the error-ridden list, though.

items.title: Transcript: Why This Veteran Election Forecaster Expects GOP “Beating”
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 3 episode of the Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

Charlie Cook has been forecasting elections for 42 years. His first political predictions were offered during Ronald Reagan’s reelection campaign in 1984. He created the Cook Political Report, which is now an institution in D.C., and he’s been talking about this election in surprising terms, as something unlike he’s ever seen before. So now that this election is upon us, we’re talking to Charlie about it. He recently retired from his life’s project, but now writes his own newsletter called Charlie Cook Politics.

We’re just going to dive right in. Charlie, it’s really good to have you on.

Charlie Cook: Thanks for having me on, Greg. And you’re right, I’ve been calling this the unicorn election. I’ve covered what, 11 midterms, 11 presidentials, and this election has dynamics I’ve never seen before. It’s some really, really unique things, of places acting like, you know, we’ve never seen before.

Sargent: We’re going to dive into all of it. I think we should start with the latest New York Times polls. They find Abdul El-Sayed up by 53 percent to 42 percent in Michigan, James Talarico up 50 to 43 in Texas, Troy Jackson up 51 to 45 in Maine, Sherrod Brown up 49 to 44 in Ohio, Adam Hamilton up 49-44 in Kansas, Mary Peltola up 48-46 in Alaska, and Josh Turek up 48-47 in Iowa.

Charlie, I and many others have a hard time believing those numbers. They seem too good to be true. That’s like wipeout proportions if those polls are right. On the other hand, it’s not implausible that they’re directionally indicating something. Charlie, do you think the Times polls are close to right?

Cook: Yes, I think they are gold standard. Absolutely. And the thing is, when you read their articles, when they have doubts about their own poll, they’re pretty clear about it. I mean, it’s like, if they are not sure these are right, they basically tell you that. And if they don’t tell you that, that means they feel very comfortable with it. But no, they’re as good as it gets.

We kind of sensed that this was headed this way. It was kind of a bifurcated election, that starting about July, August, you could—the whole nature of this race changed. It went from sort of a fairly typical midterm election, not that bad for an incumbent president’s party, but not horrible, and then it went completely in the crapper for them in August and September.

Sargent: You raise a really good point, which is that the Times write-up of these numbers didn’t signal that they think that these are outliers. And that’s, I think, probably a pretty critical tell.

Just a quick word about Texas. If you look at the Times poll, Talarico’s winning Latinos over Republican Ken Paxton by 65 to 27. Talarico is actually slightly up among non-college voters, which is a proxy for working class in our polling. And he’s winning independents by 59 to 29. That’s 30 points. That’s astounding stuff.

But Charlie, that’s how Talarico wins. He gets numbers like that among Latinos and independents and working-class voters. But that’s where the capacity for real error comes in. When you’re counting pro-Trump Latinos, those might be hard to find. Pro-Trump working-class voters, those might be hard to find. Do you think Talarico’s up seven points in Texas right now, as the Times says?

Cook: You know, I think he’s up five, six, seven. Yeah, I mean, anything above seven I would raise an eyebrow at, but I feel quite sure he’s up by more than three or four.

But no, you’re absolutely right. Now, I think a lot of people, though, their frame of reference is 2024, when that was actually kind of a low ebb for a lot of these groups for Democrats. And they were angry about inflation, they were angry about interest, they were lashing out at Biden-Harris. And so it went down in ‘24, and now it’s snapping back. Looks like it’s snapping back towards normal.

Some groups are harder to reach than others, and those are particularly hard. But for everybody that’s talking about polling error, keep in mind, the last two midterms, the two elections that Trump’s name was not literally on the ballot, the midterm polling was actually quite, quite, quite good. And the problems that we have seen in ‘16 and ‘20, ‘24—pollsters are painfully aware of it, and there’s probably just as much or greater danger of them overcompensating than there is for repeating the same mistake again.

But there are very few pollsters that don’t despise being wrong. And being wrong in the same direction in consecutive elections makes them borderline suicidal. So I would not expect to see—they may make new mistakes, but they’re not going to make those again.

Sargent: OK, so Charlie, right now, what do you think the most likely outcome in the Senate is? Where do Democrats win and where do they lose? What’s your general ballpark prediction here?

Cook: I have gone from a net gain of two or three, maybe, going into the summer, to now I’d be a little surprised if it were only four. I think it may be five, which five is the key number, because you’ve got to have a Fetterman-proof majority. And I think they’re going to get there.

And it’s a combination of Trump and the political environment on the one hand, but on the other side, you’ve got some Republicans that are really mediocre candidates. And they are running in places that they didn’t have to be any good to get there. And they’re, you know, decent enough to be fine in anything other than a really ugly year. But in an ugly year for Republicans, a Cindy Hyde-Smith is in trouble. And under these circumstances, a Roger Marshall in Kansas is in trouble. And Darline Graham.

Sargent: Democrats obviously have to net four Senate seats in order to take the majority. That would put them at 51. When you said that you expect Democrats to net five seats, you’re essentially saying that you expect them to end up at 52 seats. That’s what makes them Fetterman-proof. Earlier this summer, you thought they were going to just get into the high 40s, but now you see them getting to 52. And 52 seats and not higher, or what?

Cook: Yeah, well, I get nervous at about seven. And I’ll tell you why. I mean—but how much of this is just superstition or something, I’m not sure. Because I mean, it is absolutely true that the really close ones almost never break down the middle. They all fall—the dominoes tend to go in one direction, which would argue for a bigger number.

But at the same time, the footprint of races this year—you know, it’s not just that 20 out of the 22 Republican seats are in Trump double-digit states. But you’ve got what, six? Six are in states that haven’t voted for a Democrat for president since LBJ in ‘64. Five of them haven’t voted for a Democrat for president since Bill Clinton in ‘96.

Sargent: What you’re saying is that with the undecideds generally all kind of breaking in one direction in a lot of states at once, it’s unlikely that you see some states go one way and other states go the other way.

So if they’re going to get to 52 seats, they have a real shot at getting to 53 or 54. But on the other hand, if I understand you correctly, because they’re in such tough territory, and so many states that Trump won by double digits, you can kind of see those dominoes falling, but maybe just still not quite getting up to 53, 54 seats, right?

Cook: I guess, because this is such a red, red, red map, I get nervous trying to treat them as if they’re all purple states, because they’re not. And these are places that, you know, Democrats haven’t won since Moby Dick was a guppy. And these are people that haven’t voted Democrat in a long time. They may never again. But they are in the mood to send a message.

They are really angry, disappointed—now getting into anger at President Trump about attacking Iran and the price of energy and diesel and fertilizer, all that, and tariffs. And it’s like, they disagree with him on some big policy things. These things have hurt me and my family. And he seems to be totally preoccupied with issues that have nothing to do with me. And I think that is coming down on some people—they expect a Democratic president to screw them. They don’t expect a Republican president, this one, to screw them. But they’re feeling screwed.

Sargent: Right. These are major forces that are at work here, and really unique circumstances that have a lot of force and power.

I want to just get your bottom line. You think Democrats probably get to 52 seats, and possibly to 53 or 54. Is that right?

Cook: Yes, yes. I believe that. And I should say, these are my numbers. They’re not the Cook Political Report. You know, I’ve been gone for five years, but I agree with most of the ratings there. But yeah, these are mine. They shouldn’t be held responsible for that, for me. But yeah, I think that’s right. I mean, I think they’ll get to 52 or three. But again, that’s pre-Fetterman.

Sargent: Yeah, well, 52 gets you Fetterman-proofed, which is important.

Cook: At least, yeah. It makes you Fetterman-proof.

Sargent: So right now, let’s talk about the House. Cook Political Report has 13 GOP-held House seats as leaning Democratic, and another 14 GOP-held House seats as toss-ups. That seems astounding.

If Democrats win just the GOP-held House seats that are leaning their way, not even the toss-ups, without losing many of their own seats, they win the majority somewhat comfortably. And if they take a chunk of both those categories, of the lean-Dem category and the toss-up category, you start to see the majority getting pretty big. Can you talk about that?

Cook: Yeah, you’re absolutely right. And that’s why, having been on the inside and now on the outside—when you’re a newsletter, when you’re somebody that everybody’s watching everything you do, it tends to make you more small-c conservative.

You know, I mean, it’s like, wow, the brand’s there, it’s important, I don’t want to damage the brand. And so you don’t make a lot of willy-nilly changes.

Sargent: If you work at Cook Political Report or one of these prognosticators, you’ve got to be conservative. You can’t really go too far out on a limb, because the political world just comes down on you like a ton of bricks if you’re wrong.

I want to ask you about your piece the other day, which was very good. You identified disaffected Republicans as a key demographic to watch. These are generally reliable Republican voters who disapprove of Trump.

And a big question is, do they stay home? Do they hold their nose and vote for the Republican rather than protest Trump? Or do they maybe cross over to Democrats, right? Can you talk about this demographic and how their actions could impact the outcomes?

Cook: That says it well. We normally see—what’s the swing group perennially? It’s suburban voters, right? And particularly, like, college-educated white men, where the college-educated pulls Democrat, the male pulls Republican. Or non-college white women, where it’s exactly the opposite. That’s where we know.

But what we’re seeing here is, they’re specifically Republican, and they skew heavily rural, small town, farther out from cities. People that drive long distances in not-so-fuel—they’re not driving Rivians, OK? They’re not doing Teslas. They’re doing fairly fuel-inefficient, they use up diesel for farm equipment. But I mean, it’s all that whole energy constellation. And then the tariffs. They feel like they’re getting it straight between the eyes. And so it is a different profile.

And when you look at where these Senate races are that are behaving so curiously—Kansas, South Carolina, Mississippi, I mean, these are, even Nebraska to a certain extent—they’re not the places where you expect incredibly competitive races, and they’re not the people within those states that you usually see. So that’s why I call this a unicorn election.

Now, I don’t want to jump too far ahead, but Democrats, if they have the kind of night that I think they’re going to get, I wouldn’t want to be chair of the DCCC in 2028, having to defend a bunch of seats in places that God didn’t necessarily intend for a Democrat to hold, or the DSCC in, say, ‘34. And that puts it in more of a negative light.

Democrats have got to figure out—I mean, given the Electoral College and the U.S. Senate, they’ve got to connect again with people that live in, people call it flyover country. Rural, small town, folks that go to church regularly. These are groups that Democrats used to do pretty well with.

Sargent: And now there’s this big opening to reconnect with them right now.

Cook: Yeah, yeah.

Sargent: Charlie, where do you see the House coming down? Two hundred thirty seats, 235, 240, higher? Where do you think?

Cook: I think if you want to be conservative, you’d say 230, which Democrats are at 215 now, so 230 is 15. I frankly would take the—I’d take the over on that. I think it’s going to be over 230. But I get squeamish saying 240, 250.

Sargent: Two hundred thirty-five?

Cook: Yeah. I mean, it’s just—we’re going big, and the question is, you know, it’s like, Republican turnout is going to be low. It’s going to be really low. But how low? And Democratic turnout is going to be high, real high. African American turnout, particularly the South, I think is going to be, like, off the charts. And the extent that these things happen is where you get to really, really, really big numbers. But we’re talking about stuff that we haven’t seen in a long time. So I get nervous. I get nervous even saying it.

Sargent: Just to be sure I know where you stand. You think 230 seats for Democrats, maybe 235 seats for Democrats—

Cook: —is the realistic floor. I would be very surprised if they don’t hit that. I’d be very, very surprised.

Sargent: And then when we start talking about 240 seats for Democrats, that’s where you start to get squeamish.

Cook: Yeah, yeah, yeah. It’s asking a lot. But I mean, I was doing my column and I scratched out the word “biblical.” I mean that in terms of describing, like, the kind of losses that Republicans may be—but I did stay with, it would be the worst political environment for Republicans in at least a generation, and maybe since Watergate.

Sargent: I want to push a bit on an idea you’ve articulated, which is that this election will be decided by what you call a “red undertow.” That’s the idea, I think, that what Democrats do matters less than whether those Republicans we discussed stay home. And if they do stay home, that would pull down these GOP senators in red states. That’s the force, the red undertow you’re talking about.

But I want to ask you about this. If you look at the polling, right, the Democratic candidates are outperforming their party, and I want to ask you about that. There are these lopsided numbers among independents we talked about, which means these Democratic candidates for Senate especially are getting independents to support them.

And then, in the Times poll, Talarico is, like, running four points above the generic ballot number for Democrats. If you look at the seven Senate races the Times polled, the Senate candidates are getting around 50 percent, while the generic ballot number is a couple points below that, right? So they’re a couple points over the generic number for Democrats.

You take that plus the lopsided performance among independents, there is something happening with these—and these are some remarkable candidates as well. It seems like, Charlie, there is something happening where Democrats are winning a lot of voters to them, right?

Cook: On an individual candidate basis. You know, you could look at Adam Hamilton in Kansas and say, damn, I don’t know where the hell Democrats could have come up with a better candidate than that for example.

But it’s not—I mean, when I say it’s not a blue wave, blue wave implies Democrats, we love you and we are for everything you are, and all is forgiven for 2021, ‘22, ‘23, ‘24. That ain’t happening. This is really more about pissed off at President Trump and at Republicans who enabled him.

And so it’s a lot of that, and some Democrats in specific, running in specifically red states, that are uncannily good, and against incredibly mediocre incumbents who underperform what a potted plant might get in that state. So it’s a combination. It’s really a combination of factors. But Democrats shouldn’t—I mean, the Democratic Party’s brand isn’t any better than it was two years ago.

Sargent: Maybe the way to reconcile our positions is to say that people like Talarico and Peltola and Ossoff and Sherrod Brown, and maybe in some ways Abdul El-Sayed, and maybe a little less so Troy Jackson, but possibly Josh Turek—they’re creating an opening to fix the brand problem. Maybe that’s the way.

Because they are really staking out new territory with a new kind of voter that is generally hard for Democrats to get. And maybe that provides the opening we’re talking about for Democrats to start to reach these people in a bit more of a concerted and, I guess, salutary way.

Cook: I’m with you on each of those, except not El-Sayed, not Jackson. I’m not there. I mean, I think they’re underperformers. And not that you’ll catch me saying any good things about Haley Stevens, but had she won the primary, we wouldn’t be talking so much about Michigan right now, to be honest. And had Democrats nominated Governor Mills, we wouldn’t be talking about Maine. She would have a comfortable lead, I think, over Susan Collins.

And it’s interesting. It’s where Democrats were playing on the road, they played more small-c conservative ball, and they’re doing actually very, very well. But it’s where they had, and they knew they’d have, a home field advantage, that they started behaving in a risky way.

Sargent: So let’s just close this out. You didn’t want to use the word “biblical” to describe what you expect is going to happen to Republicans. So let’s suggest some words and maybe you can tell us what you think.

Do you think there’s going to be a big defeat for Republicans, or a modest defeat, or a rout, or a bloodbath?

Cook: What? What did Obama say, it was a thumping, and what was George W. in ‘06? How about an ass-whooping? Is that a good one? I mean, it’s more than a beating. It’s a hell of a beating.

Sargent: Right. You expect a real rout. You expect a big crushing defeat.

Cook: Yeah. Yes. Yeah. There’s no putting a smiley face on this thing.

Sargent: Charlie Cook, really, really awesome to talk to you. Thanks so much for spending that time with us.

Cook: Thanks, Greg. Anytime. Take care. Have a good one.

items.title: Is It the Dems’ Big Night? Watch These Eight Races With Early Results.
items.content_text:
One fact that’s generally true about elections is that if the wind is blowing one way in state A, it’s probably blowing in the same direction in states B, C, D, and so on. In 2024, Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris in all seven swing states. They were all close, but they all went the same way. Call it the domino theory of American elections: If one state (or district) goes a certain way, other states and districts are likely to, as well, because what voters are experiencing and thinking is not so different in Pennsylvania or Arizona.

With that in mind, here are eight races whose results we might know early that I’ll be watching as possible omens for what kind of night we can expect. All the races below are listed in this Cook Political Report web page of House races ranked by “likely R,” “lean D,” and so on. You may want to keep this handy as you settle in for the evening. Also, the bolded state and district names below link to each contest’s Ballotpedia page, where you can learn more about each than you can possibly remember.

KENTUCKY-06: Polls in the Bluegrass State close at 6 p.m., the earliest in the country (along with Indiana, although the latter crosses time zones). Kentucky’s 6th district includes Lexington (a large college town) but also a number of surrounding rural counties. The Republican incumbent is retiring, so the race features Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado. Cook gives the district a Partisan Voting Index, or PVI, of R+7, which is normally pretty safe, but this year Cook has it as a toss-up. Trump won the district by 15 points, so if Dembo wins, or even just keeps it close, that’s a good sign for the Democrats.

VIRGINIA-01: The polls close in Virginia at 7 p.m., so there’s a decent chance that we’ll start to know the results of some congressional races pretty early in the night. In Virginia’s 1st district, which hugs the Chesapeake Bay and its estuaries north of Newport News, Democrat Shannon Taylor is challenging Republican incumbent Rob Wittman. Cook has it as an R+8 district but says the race is a toss-up. Trump won the district by 5 percent two years ago, and the district hasn’t had a Democratic representative since the 1970s (though of course it has changed shape over those years due to redistricting). A Taylor win would suggest a big night.

VIRGINIA-02: Just south of the 1st, centered around Virginia Beach and Norfolk, this district is about as evenly split as any in the country—Trump won it in 2024 by 49.3 to 49.1 percent. Democrat Elaine Luria won the seat from a Republican in 2018; then she lost it to GOP incumbent Jen Kiggans in 2022. Luria is running to win it back, and Cook now rates the race “lean D.” People are mostly expecting a Luria win here. If she doesn’t, that could foretell a disappointing night.

FLORIDA-14: The Florida polls also close at 7 p.m. The state’s Republicans gerrymandered the 14th to get rid of Democrat Kathy Castor—the district was redrawn to include a lot less of Tampa and a lot more of the outlying rural counties. Trump won the areas making up this new district by 11 points. But Castor is holding her own against Republican Mike Beltran. Cook gives it an R+4 but rates it a toss-up. A Castor hold here would be an embarrassment for Governor Ron DeSantis and an indicator that Democrats should win a lot of districts like this.

FLORIDA-22: This is an open seat created by the DeSantis gerrymander. The state’s current 22nd district is represented by Democrat Lois Frankel, but she’s now running in the 23rd. So this is an open seat where Democrat Pia Dandiya faces Republican Casey Askar. This is rural southern Florida, just north of the Everglades. Cook has it at R+4 but again rates it a toss-up. A Dandiya win in this district that was created as a GOP gimme would help suggest a blue wave.

SOUTH CAROLINA-01: This is Nancy Mace’s district, which runs along the coast and includes most of Charleston. She left to run for governor (and didn’t make the runoff), so this race is between Democrat Nancy LeCore, a Navy veteran, and Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt. Cook says it’s R+6 but rates it a toss-up. There’s been one recent public poll, which LeCore led by two points. Mace served three terms, defeating a one-term Democrat who was the first of his party to hold the seat since the 1980s, so a LeCore win would really buck recent history.

That’s six to keep an eye on. Finally, here are two more in early-closing states where a Democratic win would be more of a surprise and would really suggest that a tsunami is forming.

INDIANA-05: This rural district north of Indianapolis is represented by Republican Victoria Spartz, a serious MAGA loyalist who’s faced ethics charges. Her Democratic challenger is J.D. Ford. It’s an R+8 district that Cook switched from “likely R” to “lean R” late last week.

VIRGINIA-05: And finally, here’s one that foreshadows a huge Democratic night if Tom Perriello, who represented this Charlottesville-based area for a term during the Obama years, manages to upset GOP incumbent John McGuire. It’s an R+6 district, so it’s not any different from any of the above, but Cook rates it as “likely R.”

Obviously, there are a lot of races out there that are important and that a lot more people will be interested in. I choose these only because we might know the results early, and these eight results will probably tell us what kind of night we’re in for. Fingers crossed!

items.title: How Badly Will the AfD Email Hack Hurt the German Far Right?
items.content_text:
By most accounts, Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland Party is on an upswing. It’s been steadily rising in the polls ahead of the German presidential election set to take place on January 30, 2027, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats sink, and it won the state election in Saxony-Anhalt last month while receiving the largest share of votes in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. But a recent leak of hacked emails has become a headache for the party and could give a boost to calls for it to be banned.

Hackers released more than 421,000 internal party emails and 48,000 documents dating from November 2013 to September 2026, and they have drawn comparisons to the Epstein files. To give a sense of how massive the leak is, the file is 281 gigabytes, and when I tried to download it, the torrent program estimated it would take multiple days to accomplish this feat. Less than a gigabyte in, my laptop froze.

The emails that German media have reported on thus far involve things that were already known about the party: widespread racist and neo-Nazi views among its membership; a 2017 campaign finance scandal involving co-leader Alice Weidel; and a junket by several members to Syria in 2018. But what stands out is that the emails contradict what party officials have said publicly about these matters. So, in addition to the likelihood that these emails will keep journalists busy for a while, they have also attracted attention from the Bundesamt für Verfassungsschutz, or BfV, the German domestic intelligence agency that already classifies the party as right-wing extremist.

The party did not respond to requests for comment. In an October 21 press release, the AfD confirmed the hack and said it would work with authorities to hold the perpetrators accountable. It said it would not respond to press inquiries as to whether specific content is genuine or fabricated and added that it has “already identified several concerning forgeries.” However, it did not identify what these alleged forgeries were and—showing the party’s apparent unfamiliarity with the “Streisand effect”—requested that journalists “refrain from using or disseminating any content linked to this data theft.”

Among said contents are multiple emails containing racial slurs and Nazi language, including a Christmas card with a swastika and “Heil Hitler.” This is probably the least surprising aspect of the emails for a party with a well-known track record of racism and nudge-wink Nazism.

In Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won nearly 44 percent of the vote, state party leader Ulrich Siegmund brought four former members of the Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend, a banned neo-Nazi organization modeled on the Hitler Youth, into his inner circle and has associated with people sporting clothing and tattoos with neo-Nazi symbols. The party also supports “remigration,” which means expelling people with immigrant backgrounds, even German citizens, and is regarded as a euphemism for ethnic cleansing.

In an August speech in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where it won 38.2 percent of the vote, party co-leader Tino Chrupalla drew applause from the crowd—and a criminal complaint for incitement from the Central Council of German Sinti and Roma—when he suggested a stash of guns found outside Berlin and attributed to Russian intelligence was left by “Gypsies” foraging for mushrooms, though he used the even more derogatory German-language equivalent of that word, in a political environment where anti-Romani racism, particularly among the AfD, has become “terrifyingly normalized.”

While the AfD’s racism itself isn’t necessarily remarkable, the 180-degree turn that Weidel has taken with regard to such open displays of racial animus has raised eyebrows.

Die Welt reported on October 26 that between 2015 and 2017, Weidel, then a lower-level official in the party, was worried that the “racist,” “wrong” and “problematic” views of Björn Höcke, the party leader in the eastern state of Thuringia, would cause centrist voters, particularly in the former West Germany, to “turn away from us in horror” and that his use of the term “Volksgemeinschaft”—a Nazi term for the German national community that excluded Jews and Romani people—would land the party in a BfV report, as ethno-nationalist and “völkisch” views like his blurred the lines between the AfD and the banned neo-Nazi National Democratic Party. She even tried unsuccessfully to get Höcke expelled from the AfD.

Weidel also supported the eventual expulsion from the AfD of Wolfgang Gedeon, a member of the state Parliament in Baden-Württemberg, following the 2016 discovery of his antisemitic writings, stating in an email that if Gedeon was not expelled, “we will lose members, and the AfD will shift in a direction that can no longer be controlled.”

Of course, since then, the party has very much shifted in an openly racist and fascist direction. That Höcke is an extremist cannot be overstated. He has derided the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe as a “monument of shame” while calling for Germany to abandon its policy of atonement for Nazi atrocities—much like non-German racist billionaire and AfD fanboy Elon Musk. Moreover, he has been convicted not once, but twice of using the Nazi slogan “Everything for Germany,” in a country where the public display of Nazi symbols is a crime.

The Alice Weidel who worried a decade ago about the bad taste that extremists were leaving in voters’ mouths today downplays or denies charges that the AfD is extremist while embracing Höcke and saying he would be suitable for a Cabinet position in an AfD-led government. So it appears her biggest concern was that open racists and Nazi sympathizers were a political liability, not that the AfD’s attractiveness to them signaled something fundamentally rotten about its ideology—and it looks as if that concern dissipated after the party found itself growing in the polls. Weidel’s eventual acceptance of Höcke and the almost comical hypocrisy of her personal life—as a leader of an anti-LGBTQ, xenophobic, Euro-skeptic party who is raising two children with her Sri Lankan–born same-sex partner at the home they share in Switzerland, where they can live and work freely thanks to Germany’s European Union membership—leave the impression that more than anything, Weidel is a Machiavellian opportunist.

That the leaked emails shine a light on an alleged 2017 financing scandal only deepens this impression.

Between July and September 2017, Weidel’s office received donations totaling more than 130,000 euros from Swiss-German billionaire Henning Conle, funneled through a Swiss pharmaceutical company linked to him—a violation of German campaign finance laws that forbid political parties from receiving donations from outside the EU. The party was fined 396,000 euros in 2023, and Weidel has consistently said it was only in September 2017 that she became aware of the donations. But the hacked emails suggest that she was aware of and expected the donations as early as July 2017, an allegation she has rejected.

Conle was accused in 2025 of once again making an illegal donation to the AfD—this time for 2.35 million euros through an Austrian intermediary, in violation of German laws requiring anyone who donates more than 500 euros to be publicly identified. If the allegation was confirmed, the AfD would face fines of about 7 million euros (almost $8 million).

The party gets plenty of financial support from non-billionaire affluent people too. In April 2024, Reuters profiled one wealthy AfD donor, Hartmut Issmer, then 72. One reason Issmer supported the AfD was its affinity for Russia, where he vacationed in 2023 to see beyond the “warmongering” headlines about a country that deliberately murders civilians in its unprovoked war of imperial aggression against Ukraine. Issmer returned from his vacation convinced that Russia—a predatory European colonial empire under a fascist regime that ruthlessly crushes dissent, including murdering political opponents overseas—was a model for Germany to emulate.

Pro-Russia views from the AfD cannot be written off as naïveté or the effect of seeing less litter on Russian streets than one is accustomed to at home. Under Russia’s vision of a “multipolar world,” Europe would not be a free and democratic bloc but a hodgepodge of authoritarian states subservient to Moscow or—in the case of Ukraine, Belarus, Moldova and the Baltics—recolonized by Russia. And that’s a vision that would seem to align well with the AfD’s own authoritarian, ethno-nationalist worldview and boot-licking obsequiousness toward the dictatorship of Vladimir Putin.

The party’s tongue was planted firmly on Putin’s filthy boot soles in mid-October when members of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt’s state Parliament and members of a far-left party also known for savoring the flavor of Russian shoe leather, the Bündnis Soziale Gerechtigkeit und Wirtschaftliche Vernunft, or BSW, passed a motion calling for ending aid to Ukraine and opening peace negotiations with Moscow. If enacted at the federal level, such a policy would inevitably lead to Neville Chamberlain–esque appeasement of Putin and thus encourage further Russian aggression. While symbolic, the motion was an illustrative example of a “Red-Brown Alliance,” a recurring phenomenon throughout the history of the last 100 years where the “red” hard left and “brown” fascists temporarily set aside their ideological differences to find common and usually antidemocratic cause.

Indeed, few things have illustrated the AfD’s creepy affinity for Russia more than its response to the Ukraine war.

In an interview with Economist editor in chief Zanny Minton Beddoes, Weidel claimed that Ukraine has “already lost” the war and insinuated it is not a democracy because it suspended elections in wartime—as the U.K. also did in World War II, by the way. Given that a report this month by the Institute for the Study of War showed that Russia has made almost no territorial gains despite suffering more than 1.5 million casualties, as Ukrainian drones and missiles pummel its economy, Weidel’s definition of “losing” appears rather different from that of most people.

But the hacked emails indicate the AfD’s ties with the Putin regime go much deeper than simply spouting Kremlin propaganda and opposing European efforts to stop Russia’s revanchist imperialism.

On October 24, business newspaper Handelsblatt reported that a delegation of seven AfD members visited Syria and met with officials from the now ousted Ba’athist regime of former dictator Bashar Al Assad, amid the country’s civil war in March 2018. This delegation, according to the report, likely got help crossing Syria’s border with Lebanon from the terrorist group Hezbollah and Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU, which could facilitate their entry without their needing to obtain visas beforehand.

The emails stand in stark contrast with what one of the travelers, North Rhine-Westphalia state Parliament member Christian Blex, told a press conference on the group’s return from the junket later that month, when he claimed to have applied for a visa from the Syrian Embassy in Berlin and called the suggestion by a reporter that he had received assistance from Russia “absurd.” He further suggested Syria was a “safe country of origin,” and the AfD faction of the Bundestag unsuccessfully attempted to make a motion calling for a repatriation agreement with the Assad regime.

The emails and the steady drip of media coverage that the leak has engendered will likely do little to dispel negative views of the AfD. The question that inevitably arises is, how much actual damage will these disclosures ultimately do to the party as it grows in the polls and seeks to rule the country.

Kai Arzheimer, a professor of political science at the University of Mainz, pointed out that much of what is in the emails is already known. In an email, he told me that even though revelations of a “remigration” meeting in January 2024 led to some of the largest demonstrations in postwar German history, those were “seemingly forgotten after a few months” as the AfD’s voters “seem to willingly ignore the ugly bits (and for some of them, they’re part of the attraction).”

With respect to a ban, Arzheimer said, the impact is also unclear. The legal question is whether all of this is characteristic of the party as a whole—and it’s one the emails likewise leave unanswered. Lawyers at Germany’s Society for Civil Rights see a ban as likely successful from a legal standpoint, stating in a report in June that the party is “demonstrably unconstitutional.” But Arzheimer said the more relevant question is political—that is to say, whether the government will find the courage to enact a ban while it still can.

“There is of course a chance that the current leak may sway the public’s view of the AfD, which could help the government to find said courage,” he told me. “But with news cycles being what they are, I suspect that public and media attention may have moved on to something else in a few weeks’ time.”

items.title: Bernie Sanders Is on the Ballot—Against Trump
items.content_text:
Bernie Sanders is drawing massive crowds, not in the so-called “Commie Corridor” of Brooklyn and Queens, but in battleground states like Maine, Florida, and Michigan. This is unusual, as Atlantic writer Russell Berman noted earlier this week: “Democratic candidates typically embrace him during primaries and then stick him on the sidelines for the stretch run, when they’re rediscovering their love of capitalism and bipartisanship.” But this year, many of these candidates are still embracing him—and his policies—in the general election, despite competing in tight races against Republicans. By doing so, they’re testing a long-running question on the left: Can Democrats beat Republicans with a social-democratic platform centered on the working class? Tuesday’s elections will provide a clearer answer than any U.S. election has this century.

When Sanders ran for president in 2016 and 2020, many of his supporters insisted that had he won the Democratic primary, he would have gone on to win the general election. In this dreamy hypothetical scenario, we could have been spared Trump in 2016 (perhaps also averting Biden, the genocide in Gaza, and Trump 2.0). “Bernie would have won!” has been a wistful core belief of the Vermont senator’s supporters; some poll data indeed suggests he could have, but given all the oligarchic cash that would have been deployed to oppose him, the unpredictability of polling, and the conservativism of many Americans, who knows? We never will, of course. Sanders is (presumably!) too old to run for president again, so these midterms are the best test yet of whether his politics can beat Trumpism on the ballot.

The core of Sanders’s politics is an opposition to oligarchy and support for a better life for America’s working class. In policy terms, that has meant support for Medicare for All, lowering the price of prescription drugs, taxing the rich and large corporations, limiting corporate power, the right to organize unions, and free college. It has also meant universal childcare, the right to choose abortion, affordable housing, a higher minimum wage, fully funded K-12 public schools, and an end to most foreign wars. Some version of this agenda has exploded all over the country, with great success, electing mayors, congresspeople, city councilmembers, and state legislators, mostly in blue areas. But only now are its powers being seriously tested on red and purple terrain in races of national significance.

In Maine, Democratic voters, eager to run a Sanders-style Democrat against incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins, nominated Graham Platner, a charismatic oysterman and former Marine who supported Medicare for All. When Platner dropped out over sexual assault allegations, he was replaced, in a complicated internal party process, by Troy Jackson, a former logger and labor leader. Jackson’s personality is far less colorful than Platner’s, but his politics are similar. The issue atop Jackson’s platform is Medicare for All; after that, lowering the price of prescription drugs and taxing billionaires and large corporations. The race is close, with Jackson leading slightly.

By now everyone has heard of Abdul El-Sayed, who first burst onto the Michigan political scene in 2018 to run for governor, a doctor fighting for Medicare for All who was one of the first candidates to be embraced by Sanders’s movement as a “Berniecrat.” He lost in 2018, but this time, running for Senate with a message of “Money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all,” he’s commanded far more momentum. This race is also very close.

Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Florida, is prioritizing Medicare for All too, followed by universal childcare, public education, housing, and unions. She’s polling several points behind Republican Ashley Moody. But even if Nixon loses, no one should write her off—nor underestimate the future of Sanders-style politics in her state: She leads with 68 percent among voters 18–25, and 59 percent among those age 25–34.

There’s an important caveat here: Each of those candidates has put some distance between themselves and the socialist movement. El-Sayed says he is not a socialist, Jackson hasn’t used that word, and Nixon is a member of Democratic Socialists of America but says she herself is not a democratic socialist. But they are running on the same issues Sanders ran on, and Sanders has appeared on the campaign trail with each of them.

There are many other races in purple and red areas around the country where Sanders’s influence can be felt. Smoke jumper and union leader Sam Forstag in Montana’s deep-red 1st congressional district is running against Republican Aaron Flint in a competitive open race, on a vow to “Make Montana Work for Working People,” with housing, health care, childcare and education at the top of his platform. Will Lawrence, in Michigan’s 7th congressional district, which went slightly for Trump in 2024, is polling ahead of incumbent Republican Tom Barrett. Lawrence is running on taxing the rich, affordable housing, and health care for all.

Then there’s Nevada, a state where Sanders won the 2020 Democratic presidential caucus in a landslide. Many of his followers have described that night as the last time they had any hope for a leftist turn in national politics. This year, working-class Latino voters may hand the Democrats a victory over an incumbent Republican governor and flip a House seat in a red district, thanks in part to Sanders’s playbook. In an interview with Politico, Democratic Senator Catherine Cortez Mastro emphasized Nevada’s lessons for Democrats across the country: Focus on the cost of living. The gubernatorial Democratic challenger, Aaron Ford, is running on an “Affordable Nevada” platform with housing and health care as the top two issues. The first sentence of House candidate Teresa Bentiz Thompson’s platform is, “People across northern Nevada are working harder and getting less.”

Whether or not these candidates win will not decisively settle the question about whether Sanders-style politics can topple Trumpism in elections. There are too many other electoral factors in play, from the president’s corruption to ICE’s abuses.
