Since Roe v. Wade was overturned by the Supreme Court’s conservative supermajority in June 2022, abortion has become a nonstop losing streak for Republicans, pitting the party’s long-standing policies against their increasingly dire ramifications.

States that enforced aggressive abortion restrictions saw medical brain drains, with large swaths of medical professionals moving elsewhere. Other states with such rules witnessed the horrific reality of allowing the legislature into the doctor’s office (see: the case of Adriana Smith, a Georgia nurse who died in 2025 but nonetheless was forced to remain on life support as an incubation chamber after doctors discovered a nine-week fetus in her abdomen. Her family had no say in that matter).

The bad PR has led to a quiet stripping of pro-life policies from conservative platforms across the country, with the GOP futilely attempting to ditch the “pro-life” branding altogether in an effort to skirt more electoral losses.

National surveys indicate that the vast majority of the country supports abortion access. In a poll published by the Pew Research Center in March, 60 percent of respondents said abortion should be legal in pretty much all cases, while only 38 percent said it should be illegal in most cases.

items.title: So Who’s Running the Party Now: Progressives or Moderates?
items.content_text:
You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.


Inside Washington

Democrats have won a massive majority in the House, and amid the celebrations, different factions of the party will be clamoring to claim credit for the blue tsunami. Was it the progressives, the centrists, or even the Bernie dogs who carried the party to victory? And which faction will be calling the shots come January?

The answer, to some extent, depends on who you ask. “A Democratic majority is really going to be built on the back of moderate candidates in the House,” said David de la Fuente, deputy director for politics and research at the centrist group Third Way. He pointed to moderate candidates who eventually won on Tuesday night, like Jared Moskowitz in Florida’s 25th congressional district or Bobby Pulido in Texas’s 15th congressional district.

Meanwhile, Usamah Andrabi, the communications director of progressive group Justice Democrats, argued that progressives brought the energy and policy platforms that turned the tide. “The mandate from voters across this country is for this majority to look like what many Democrats finally learned to campaign on, which is taking on corporate interests to deliver on an affordability agenda that actually helps working class communities,” he said. “They finally listened to the left.”

Andrabi pointed to Justice Democrats’ massive wins this cycle; it was their most successful year by far. The group is poised to send at least seven leaders to Congress, including Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York, and Melat Kiros in Colorado. These electeds will be joining fellow progressive firebrands like Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, and Greg Casar in Congress. As it stands, the Congressional Progressive Caucus currently has 101 members, while the New Democrat Coalition, which includes more centrist lawmakers, touts 114 members. While it’s too soon to say definitively how those numbers will change, the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC suggested that the caucus might be adding “over 20” new members, according to an email the group sent previewing a later press call.

“Typically, the Congressional Progressive Caucus is bigger than the New Dems when Republicans control the House, and the New Dems are bigger than the progressives when the Democrats control the House, and that’s because, essentially, the New Dems tend to be the majority makers,” de la Cruz said. The term “majority maker” comes from former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who famously called the moderate-to-conservative Blue Dogs the “majority makers” for their success in unseating Republicans and contributing to the Democratic majority.

But some progressive candidates overturned that orthodoxy on Tuesday. In Michigan’s 7th congressional district, Sunrise Movement co-founder William Lawrence prevailed despite running in one of the most competitive districts in the county, and facing the most Republican spending of any House candidate this cycle—more than $23 million. Similarly, in California’s 22nd congressional district, Randy Villegas declared an early victory over Republican Representative David Valadao, a testament to the size of his win (usually, California results trickle in slowly).

Trying to tally up the number of seats that will soon be held by progressives versus moderates creates another problem: “It suggests that there’s just a kind of monolithic progressive ideology and a monolithic centrist ideology, and in my experience, it’s not quite that simple,” Democratic strategist Oliver Libby said.

This year, that question became even more complicated with the emergence of a number of so-called Bernie dogs—candidates endorsed by both the Blue Dogs and Senator Bernie Sanders. Those candidates include Sam Forstag in Montana’s 1st congressional district, Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin’s 3rd congressional district, Brian Poindexter in Ohio’s 7th district, and Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania’s seventh district. All four won.

A more useful way of analyzing the Democratic majority—and predicting what they might do come January—could be to look directly at what policies they ran on, regardless of how they identify ideologically. That could help reconcile the simultaneous successes of moderates, progressives, and Bernie dogs, the Progressive Change Campaign Committee suggested in an Election Day memo. These winning policy platforms—including anti-establishment fights against data centers and surveillance tech, oversight of AI companies, and affordable health care—could ultimately provide a roadmap for Dems in 2028 and beyond.

—Emma Janssen


Outside Washington

The humble “I Voted” sticker could turn out to be one of the enduring images of this election. On October 19—the first day of early voting in Texas—Ronaldo Salgado cast a ballot and placed his voting sticker on Houston’s makeshift memorial to his father, who was shot and killed by an ICE officer this summer. Amid a historic rise in early voting, hundreds of other voters proceeded to follow Salgado’s lead, leaving “I Voted” stickers or other messages at the memorial to Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. On Tuesday afternoon, MPR News and other outlets reported that the practice had spread to Minneapolis, with local affiliate Fox 9 reporting “dozens” of “I Voted” stickers at the memorials for Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by an ICE agents in January.

Elsewhere:

  • James Talarico, Gina Hinojosa, and Nathan Johnson won the Senate, gubernatorial, and attorney general races in Texas last night—breaking a 32-year Dem losing streak in statewide races. But if we’re talking long losing streaks: No Democrat has held a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission—an underappreciated body with huge and little understood power to regulate the fossil fuel industry—since 1990. On Tuesday, though, Democrat Jon Rosenthal claimed victory over Republican Bo French, a candidate so prone to nakedly racist rhetoric that even Karl Rove denounced him in The Wall Street Journal in September and vowed to vote for Rosenthal.
  • As of publication time for this newsletter, the race in New Jersey’s 2nd congressional district has not been called. Multiple outlets have reported, however, that four-term Republican Representative Jeff Van Drew has conceded to Democrat Zack Mullock. This is another race that longtime watchers of Democratic politics are going to be talking about today—particularly if a formal winner emerges. You can read more about this race—Van Drew, who used to be a Democrat, “has certainly earned the everlasting animosity of Democrats in the district,” Micah Rasmussen said—in Emma Janssen’s prior TNR Blue Book reporting here. Just a few weeks ago when this was written, analysts that she talked to still thought a Mullock victory was a long shot. Early Wednesday morning, Mullock led by nearly 8,000 votes, with 92 percent in.

—Heather Souvaine Horn


In Closing

Political Trivia Question of the Day  

If Scott Colom wins in Mississippi, he’ll be the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, when two Black men were elected to the Senate from the state. Can you name either? (Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

items.title: Washington State Votes to Keep Making Millionaires Pay Their Share
items.content_text:
Washington voters decided to keep their state’s millionaire tax on Tuesday.

Fifty-eight percent of Washingtonians voted against Initiative 645, an effort to repeal the state’s millionaire tax led by right-wing donors and PACs, including Let’s Go Washington. The PAC, headed by conservative hedge fund executive Brian Heywood, was the most active group in the $13.1 million failed effort to overturn the 9.9 percent tax on income over $1 million a year.

“I can’t tell you how many people have left the state,” Heywood told The Guardian in October. “My business partner moved to Arizona. I probably know 50 people that are deca- or centi-millionaires that have left the state.”

The millionaire tax, which was signed into law in March, uses the funding to expand eligibility for the Working Families Tax Credit, allowing 460,000 more households a cash rebate of up to $1,330.

items.title: Congrats to the First Muslim Senator, First Gay Senator, and More
items.content_text:
Americans made history Tuesday night. Amidst the seasonal pandemonium of ballot counting and number crunching, the country elected several political firsts.

Michigan elected its first Muslim senator, choosing Dr. Abdul El-Sayed over Republican candidate Mike Rogers. El-Sayed ran a shrewd campaign, canvassing across the state and overcoming a nasty strain of Islamophobia while holding earnest, intelligent conversations with conservatives and liberals alike.

Halfway across the country, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won her bid for Georgia’s gubernatorial office, making her the first Black woman to hold a governorship in U.S. history. Her winning campaign platform promised to push back on the White House, to find relief for inflated gas and grocery prices, to eliminate state income tax for public school teachers, and to impose a moratorium on data center development.

In Illinois, voters chose to send Juliana Stratton to the Senate. Stratton’s admittance to the upper chamber in January will mark the first time in U.S. history that three Black women have served in the Senate simultaneously. She joins Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland. The previous record was set in 2025, when Blunt Rochester and Alsobrooks joined the 119th Congress.

Nearby, Ohioans elected Dr. Amy Acton as their first woman governor, besting billionaire tech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy. Ramaswamy’s final campaign push centered around a disturbing ad that featured Acton’s estranged mother declaring that something was wrong with the 60-year-old Democrat.

She wasn’t the only gubernatorial first. Deb Haaland, who served as secretary of the interior under former President Joe Biden, became the first Native woman to be elected governor when New Mexicans cast their ballots Tuesday.

The diversity achievements also extended to Texas, where civil rights attorney Gina Hinojosa became the first Latina governor in the nation.

Other candidates that broke the mold include former Minnesota state Representative Peggy Flanagan, who became the first Native woman to be elected to the U.S. Senate. The Native community’s groundbreaking moment could be made that much sweeter by a win for former Representative Mary Peltola, who is currently fractions of a percentage point behind Republican Dan Sullivan for Alaska’s Senate seat as the Last Frontier continues to tabulate its ballots.

Delivering a speech from St. Paul, Minnesota, Flanagan noted that her victory signaled a breakthrough in the nationwide fight against Donald Trump’s MAGA movement.

“You said no more war. No more health care cuts. No more taking away food from children and seniors. No more selling this country off to the highest bidder. And no more masked goons shooting our neighbors,” Flanagan said, according to the Minnesota Reformer.

And nearly 50 years after Harvey Milk was elected as the country’s first openly gay lawmaker, New Hampshire elected former Representative Chris Pappas as the first openly gay man to become a U.S. senator.

items.title: Maryland Democrats Land Massive Win on Voting Maps
items.content_text:
Maryland voters approved a ballot measure Tuesday amending the state’s Constitution to allow Democratic-led congressional redistricting.

The measure, known as Question 3, passed 60 percent to 40 percent, with 77 percent of votes counted.

The measure does not enact a new map, but gives Maryland state legislators greater powers in drawing congressional district boundaries. Maryland has eight congressional districts, and all but one, the 1st district, are represented by a Democrat. The state Constitution currently requires compact districts that respect “natural boundaries,” and the 1st district, represented by Republican Andy Harris, is mostly confined to Maryland’s eastern side of the Chesapeake Bay.

Republicans fought the ballot question in court, but in September, the state Supreme Court allowed the amendment to be put to a vote in November’s elections. In the weeks leading up to the election, Maryland’s Democratic Governor Wes Moore campaigned for the measure, and former President Barack Obama lent his endorsement, filming a video ad urging voters to approve it.

Missouri also voted on redistricting Tuesday night, and the Show Me State’s residents blocked a Republican-led effort to gerrymander the state in favor of conservatives.

Last year, Donald Trump began pushing Republican-led states to gerrymander their districts in order to prevent a Democratic majority in Congress from investigating him. This set off a gerrymandering war, and Republicans successfully put new maps in place in seven states: Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Ohio. That was helped by the Supreme Court gutting the Voting Rights Act in April, allowing Southern states to eliminate majority-Black districts.

Until now, Democrats only had one successful redistricting effort in California and a favorable ruling from a federal judge in Utah, who rejected a Republican-drawn map in favor of independent redistricting reform approved by voters in 2018, creating another Democratic district. For 2028, it appears that Democrats are on their way to picking up another congressional seat in Maryland.

items.title: Swing State Voters Reject Trump-Backed Effort to Steal House Seats
items.content_text:
Missourians blocked a new congressional map pushed by the state’s Republicans and President Donald Trump Tuesday by nearly 62 percent of the vote.

Proposition A would have redrawn the state’s map to favor Republicans and push Democratic Representative Emanuel Cleaver, whose district currently comprises most of Kansas City along with nearby suburbs, out of office. The vote follows months of television ads mostly opposing the new map drawn by Republicans last year, according to St. Louis Public Radio.

Republicans tried to force their new map through before the midterms, but the Supreme Court halted their efforts in an unsigned order in September. In the months since then, Democrats successfully canvassed across Missouri in an effort to defeat the measure, while Republicans, who were hoping to have the map in place already, had less enthusiasm.

Trump began pushing for rapid redistricting last year in an effort to keep a Republican majority in Congress and prevent Democratic investigations of himself and his administration. That set off a gerrymandering war, with Republicans successfully getting new maps in place in seven states: Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Ohio. The effort was helped by the Supreme Court gutting the Voting Rights Act in April, allowing Southern states to eliminate majority-Black districts.

Democrats were only able to respond with one successful redistricting effort in California, and picked up a seat in Utah thanks to a federal judge rejecting a Republican-drawn map in favor of independent redistricting reform approved by voters in 2018. In Missouri Tuesday, voters sided with Democrats, but the redistricting fight will continue there and across the country for 2028’s presidential election.

items.title: Trump Tries to Blame Everyone But Himself for Democratic Sweep
items.content_text:
Donald Trump demanded that the midterm elections be another referendum on his popularity, but now he can’t seem to accept the results.

The president called in to Fox News around midnight to complain about the conservative media behemoth’s polls, which reflected Trump’s tanking approval ratings.

“And then I read at Fox that I’m not popular. The Fox polls are terrible. You ought to get yourself a good pollster ‘cause your polls are the worst,” Trump said live on air.

Host Brett Baier pushed back: “But tonight, actually, the results are pretty close to what the Fox polls showed.”

But Trump wasn’t willing to confront reality. “Well, I don’t know about that,” he snipped.

Democrats won big all over the country—even in historically deep red districts—taking control of both chambers of Congress in the process. Despite the obvious blow, Trump told Fox News that he had the “greatest two years in the history of the presidency.”

An NBC News exit poll found that more than half of voters saw the election as an opportunity to rebuke Trump and his MAGA agenda, which has thus far included an aggressive foreign policy that tied Americans to a wildly unpopular war with Iran, economic tariffs that vastly inflated the cost of living, and a militaristic deportation scheme that has pitted federal agents against the general population.

Republican candidates saw the writing on the wall months ago, but were unable to successfully peel their campaigns away from the president’s influence. Instead, the president urged voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” By late Tuesday, Trump was already trying to rewrite history.

In a separate interview Tuesday night, Trump told Politico’s Dasha Burns that his party would have won big if he was on the ballot.

“I wasn’t on the ballot, and we didn’t get the people out, but I wasn’t on the ballot,” Trump said. “If I was on the ballot, we would have won. We would have won it all very easily.”

“But Mr. President, you told voters that you were on the ballot, to vote as though you were on the ballot,” Burns reminded him.

“I said, ‘Think about me being on the ballot,’ but they didn’t agree and they didn’t like the candidates in most cases. Just one of those things,” Trump said.

He then offered that he didn’t want to blame any one individual, but that he watched the results roll in with “great interest” and that he “learned from it.”

“What did you learn, sir?” Burns pressed.

“Well, we’re going to work with the Democrats, to make sure things go well for our country. They’ve already called and—I have the right to veto everything, but I don’t want be just sitting there vetoing everything,” Trump said. “We have a lot of friends in the Democratic Party.”

items.title: Elon Musk Spirals Over His Failure to Buy Elections
items.content_text:
After wasting almost half a billion dollars supporting Republicans in the midterm elections, tech oligarch Elon Musk is having trouble digesting the Democratic landslide.

Musk took to his X platform in the early hours Wednesday morning, offering some lame observations as his preferred candidates were trounced. At about 1:12 am, Musk posted, “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” before following that up with, “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time 🤷‍♂️” a minute later.

A couple of hours later, he commented, “Interesting” on a repost of exit polling purporting to show that voters supported the Trump administration’s immigration policies, but massively opposed the Iran war.

It’s not clear where that polling is from or whether it is credible, but in any case, Musk appears to be trying to cope with the negative results as best as he can. Stocks in his Tesla and SpaceX companies are plummeting Wednesday despite other tech companies doing well in early trading. His plan to merge SpaceX and Tesla might now hit some obstacles in a Democratic-controlled Congress, which has already signaled that investigations of the tech oligarch are on the way.

Plus, Musk moved his companies from California to Texas to escape Democratic oversight, only to now have a Democratic governor in the Lone Star State, Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned against Musk. She also called for a moratorium on new data centers and an end to tax breaks for the industry. Now Democrats in Texas, as well as across the country, have him and other tech barons in their crosshairs.

“They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” posted Democratic Senator Ed Markey Tuesday night.

items.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Victory Is Historic for These Two Reasons
items.content_text:
Abdul El-Sayed’s election is a watershed moment in American politics. The victory of a devout Muslim, particularly in a fairly white, moderate state like Michigan, is another step toward America becoming a truly multicultural democracy. And the triumph of a progressive candidate in a swing state, despite intense opposition from Republicans and centrist Democrats—particularly his primary opponent Representative Haley Stevens—suggests that conventional notions of what kinds of candidates are “electable” should be further discarded. 

El-Sayed is the first Muslim American ever elected to the Senate. There will probably never be a large number of Muslim senators, since followers of Islam are only around 1 percent of the U.S. population. But being Muslim is arguably a bigger barrier to success in America, particularly in electoral politics, than being Black, Latino, female, gay, or a member of another group whose members often face discrimination. Anti-Muslim sentiment in America is actively stoked by the political right and in many ways tolerated by the rest of our society. In a recent Pew Research Center poll, 42 percent of American adults said that Muslims have a negative impact on the United States, 43 percent said Muslims are less patriotic than other Americans. Fifty-one percent said that Islam encourages violence more than other religions, including 76 percent of Republicans and, yes, 29 percent of Democrats. 

In Michigan, 39 percent of voters said that a candidate being Muslim makes them less likely to vote for that person, according to an October survey conducted by the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research at Michigan State University. In contrast, only 10 percent said they were less likely to vote for female candidates. These numbers likely vastly underestimate Islamophobia, since some who hold these views might be leery of acknowledging them to a stranger calling from a polling company. 

Islamophobia has been a powerful force affecting the most important political figures of this era. In his 2008 campaign, Barack Obama, who spent some of his childhood in heavily Muslim Indonesia and whose middle name is Hussein, repeatedly emphasized that he is not Muslim, no doubt aware that Islamophobia is even more widespread than anti-Black racism in America. Obama’s successor, Donald Trump, rose to power in part by promising during his first campaign to limit the number of Muslims entering America, casting their mere presence as a danger to the country. 

Trump won in 2016 even as the media openly called his proposal a “Muslim ban.” And in both of his terms, Trump’s administration has intentionally restricted immigration from majority-Muslim countries, with little pushback from Dems, the national media, or voters. 

El-Sayed was facing both that backdrop of anti-Muslim sentiment and specific tensions around his religion throughout his campaign. Trump and Republicans constantly implied he was supportive of terrorism and potentially even a terrorist himself. The news media repeatedly asked El-Sayed about the Muslim Brotherhood and other issues related to his faith that were not relevant to the Michigan primary. 

A significant bloc of Democrats slammed his relationship with political commentator Hasan Piker, and his positions on Israeli-Palestinian policy, namely El-Sayed describing Israel’s war in Gaza as a genocide, calling for a suspension of U.S. military aid to Israel, and questioning the idea of a state where Jewish people always have political control over Palestinians. Some claimed he was insufficiently concerned about antisemitism. 

Perhaps these Democrats would have celebrated a pro-Israel Muslim candidate, or at least a candidate who sidestepped the issue. But it’s hard to disentangle these critiques from El-Sayed’s faith. American Muslims are deeply concerned about Israel’s actions in Gaza over the last three years, so expecting Muslims politicians to soft-pedal that issue is asking them to essentially deny their Muslim identity. The party establishment also regularly undermines and lodges antisemitism accusations at Zohran Mamdani, Ilhan Omar, and Rashida Tlaib, three of the other most prominent Muslim politicians in America. 

A week before the election, former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, both a party elder and supposedly deeply committed to fighting Republicans, blasted El-Sayed over his Israel views and hinted that he would lose because of them. The party got fully behind El-Sayed only two days before the election, after Stevens’s shocking decision to actually endorse Republican Mike Rogers. 

El-Sayed overcame all of that. The main reason he won is that Democrats everywhere did, as the election was a backlash against Trump. But that doesn’t take away from the importance of his victory. Obama won in  2008 in large part because of hatred of George W. Bush and the Iraq War, but America electing a Black person president was still a major step forward in our democracy. A Muslim candidate winning a swing state shows that many Americans, particularly Democrats, truly want us to be a nation based on our shared ideals and values, not a country dominated by white people, men, and/or Christians. 

The resistance to El-Sayed, from both Republicans and some Democrats, of course, wasn’t just about religion or Israel policy. El-Sayed has long been aligned with Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and others in the party’s progressive wing. The party’s left backed his 2018 gubernatorial primary against center-left favorite and eventual Governor Gretchen Whitmer. 

In the Senate primary earlier this year, the party’s center-left largely backed Stevens and hinted that El-Sayed could not win a general election. Progressives went all in for El-Sayed. They wanted an ally in the Senate. But they also wanted to prove that a fairly progressive candidate could win in a swing state like Michigan. Centrist Democrats constantly say progressive views and politicians should be ignored because the left doesn’t understand how to win elections and therefore keep Republicans out of power. 

Game changed. A candidate calling for Medicare for All and fighting billionaires while welcoming Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders to campaign for him in the general election has won Michigan, the quintessential swing state. And several other progressive candidates won in swing districts and states too. This is a big blow to centrist arguments about electability. And they know it—prominent center-left Democrats spent the weeks ahead of the election demanding that El-Sayed win by as much as more centrist candidates in Michigan and around the country or they would diminish his win. That discrediting will be less effective after Stevens spent the days right before the election actively trying to defeat El-Sayed. She proved progressives’ arguments that centrists’ electability claims are often a pretext to mask their deep ideological opposition to progressive politicians and causes. 

One direct result of the Michigan results is that I expect Ocasio-Cortez to run for president. El-Sayed and others who won in swing districts and states ran on the anti-billionaire, working class–centered approach that the New York congresswoman has helped pioneer. Those victories will help Ocasio-Cortez rebut arguments that she could not win a general election. And the party’s progressive wing will likely want to push its own candidates at a time when it appears as if the electorate is deeply skeptical of billionaires and Republicans and might consider more nontraditional candidates. 

“Democrats everywhere, including moderates in swing seats, are running ads centered around a pro-working class message, opposing billionaires, foreign wars, corruption, and corporations,” said Evan Brown, executive director of the Congressional Progressive Caucus’s PAC, in a memo released on the eve of the election. 

Even if Ocasio-Cortez doesn’t launch a presidential campaign in the next few months, El-Sayed’s victory opens up new possibilities. Or more accurately, he reminds us that these possibilities exist. No one expected Obama and Trump to be elected president a few years before they were. Despite the confident claims of pundits and center-left Democrats, politics is not an exact science. A left-wing man named Abdul becoming the senator from Michigan doesn’t just prove that progressives or Muslims can be elected but that timing and circumstance really matter. Perhaps the next president will be Ocasio-Cortez. Or perhaps it’s someone none of us are thinking about right now. 

This is not 2008. Abdul El-Sayed will not be running the country. But even more than Obama, El-Sayed overcame deep skepticism about his faith, policy positions, identity, and patriotism—including from many Democrats. The biggest story of November 2026 is Democrats winning across the country, including in red states like Nebraska. But another huge story is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed’s triumph in a country that twice elected Donald Trump.

items.title: Trump Presidency on Life Support after Blue Tsunami’s Reach Shocks GOP
items.content_text: In a stunning series of outcomes, Democrats won control of the House and Senate on Tuesday. They’re projected to take control of at least 244 House seats, per NBC, and as of now, they’ve flipped Senate seats in South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, and Maine. That means they’ll control at least 54 seats. But what also makes these results stunning is how Democrats captured a lot of new territory in places they’ve long struggled to reach. They made huge inroads into the South, won a Senate seat in the Great Plains, and reached deep into the parts of the Midwest that we all thought Trump had turned permanently red. We talked to New Republic editor Michael Tomasky about all of it. We discuss how Trump brought his party to this disastrous moment, how these Democratic gains will alter our political geography, what this all portends for JD Vance, how a new Democratic Party may be coming into being, and how it will handle a severely diminished Trump next year. Listen to this episode here. A transcript is here.

items.title: Say Goodnight, New Democrats. It’s the Era of the New New Democrats.
items.content_text:
There are about a thousand takeaways from a historic election like this one, the chief one being the thorough, and thoroughly gratifying, repudiation of you-know-who. But I’m going to focus on the one that gets at the heart of a key question for Democrats about what kind of party they’re going to be, heading into 2028 and beyond. And the lesson is this: With Tuesday’s election results, particularly the Senate victories of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas, the 1990s centrist rules about how you win a Senate race in a purple or red state are dead.

The ’90s gave birth to the so-called “New Democrats,” the centrists who’d jettisoned the old liberalism and adopted a more corporate-friendly aspect. For decades, you had to be a New Democrat to be taken seriously. But this week, we entered a new era.

El-Sayed and Talarico were never supposed to win these races. Talarico took positions in the past—notably on transgender rights, an issue that is supposed to be poison for Democrats—that the ’90s conventional wisdom would say there’s no way he could overcome, especially in deep-red Texas. El-Sayed was vehemently opposed by establishment Democrats, some of them because of his views on Israel, but many (and, in my anecdotal experience, most) of them on the grounds that he was too far left and absolutely unelectable in a swing state like Michigan. I had a number of conversations with Washington Democrats earlier this year in which I heard it said that if he was nominated, the party was just giving that Senate seat away.

But both candidates ran as aggressive economic populists, attacking billionaires and vowing to fight on behalf of working-class people. El-Sayed was ceaselessly on-message: Money out of politics, money in your pockets, Medicare for All. And Talarico, while he did walk back some of his more progressive stands on cultural issues, never wavered on economics and delivered what for my money was the single most memorable riff of the campaign: “The only minority destroying America is the billionaires. We are focused on the wrong one percent. Trans people aren’t taking away our health care. Muslims aren’t defunding our schools. Immigrants aren’t cutting taxes for themselves and their rich friends. It’s the billionaires and their puppet politicians.”

People who talk like that aren’t supposed to win Senate seats. But they both won and won fairly handily. Those inclined to disagree with my thesis will jump in and point out how lucky the candidates were. Talarico faced a uniquely appalling opponent. El-Sayed faced an uncharismatic opponent and gained ground after Haley Stevens’s Wagnerian self-immolation over the weekend. And of course, they benefited from Trump’s massive unpopularity and a bad economy.

Fine. All that’s true. On the other hand: Both had some $200 million thrown into vicious attacks on them and their character. Talarico was unmasculine, gay, nonbinary, whatever. El-Sayed was a jihadist, even a terrorist. And according to the old Democratic conventional wisdom, those attacks are supposed to work.

But they failed. And from this day forward, no one in the Democratic Party can credibly argue that the only way to win a Senate seat in a purple or red state is to nominate a corporate, cautious, centrist Democrat. You might say the Erskine Bowles era is over.

Who? Erskine Bowles was a good Democrat—of his time. He was a chief of staff in the Clinton White House. After Clinton left office, Democrats in his home state of North Carolina needed a known-name candidate to run for Senate against Elizabeth Dole. He was exactly the kind of candidate the Democrats of that era wanted—a white, moderate businessman from a Tarheel State political family who’d buffed and shined his corporate credentials, in his case spending years at Morgan Stanley.

Dole swamped him, by nine points. Two years later, he took one more shot. That time, he came a little closer, but he still lost to Richard Barr by nearly five points. Later, during the Obama era, Bowles co-chaired a commission that advised Obama to stop all that liberal spending nonsense and attack the deficit. Over the years, he’s sat on the boards of Morgan Stanley, General Motors, Norfolk Southern, and—dum da dum dum—Facebook.

I don’t mean to pick on Bowles. I single him out because he’s emblematic of the kind of person the Washington Democratic establishment types all agreed in their wisdom for three decades the party simply had to put forward for the Senate in swing states (in fact, even in many blue states). The national political media, by the way, by and large parroted this line.

They weren’t always wrong at the time. There were plenty of moderates who won Senate races in swing states. And of course some moderates will still win such races, as indeed some have in these midterms. But the point is that, as of Tuesday, that’s not the only way to skin the cat. And this is a hugely important development.

If El-Sayed can win in Michigan and Talarico can win in Texas, it means that economic populists can win in a lot of places where Democratic conventional wisdom said they could never win. It means that come 2028, when populist Democrats are running in Senate primaries in Wisconsin or Iowa or North Carolina or Florida or maybe even Missouri—all states where Republican incumbent senators will be up for reelection two years hence—no one can say they can’t possibly win.

It’s an absolute sea change inside the Democratic Party—the erasure of 30 years of conventional wisdom that’s been running on fumes for at least 10 of those years—and it means that by 2029, if there’s a Democratic president and the party controls both houses of Congress, they may actually have a critical mass of legislators who are ready to fight for working people.

items.title: Trumpism Is Failing Because It Is Very, Very Stupid
items.content_text:
The 2026 midterms are over, which means that the 2028 presidential election is now underway. President Donald Trump occasionally jokes that he would run for a third term despite the Constitution’s two-term limit. The reality is that Republicans will need to find a new front-runner over the next two years.

This will be a fraught moment for their coalition. Trump’s approval ratings are in the low 30s. The Iran war remains insoluble. Trump cannot achieve victory through conventional strength of arms. He lacks the credibility and temperament to reach a permanent agreement with Tehran. The Iranian government, for its part, seems content to watch high oil prices choke the life out of the American economy.

There will be a temptation for Republicans to propose doing Trumpism the right way, to achieve their goals without the errors that beset Trump’s second term. This is a fool’s errand. Trump’s mistakes were not a deviation from Trumpism; they were Trumpism. His political movement is, at its core, based on a rejection of knowledge and expertise. As a result, it is inherently self-destructive.

The problem began in 2016. Trump’s first term was a fluke. The president and his allies were not expecting to win the election. Trump repeatedly cast doubt on the integrity of the results before Election Day to soften the ground for his anticipated defeat. His team was reportedly shocked that they narrowly won enough votes in key states to eke out a narrow victory in the Electoral College.

As a result, Trump and his team put minimal effort into mapping out what his first term would look like until it was necessary. The president was still a relative newcomer to the party infrastructure and had to rely on more experienced Republicans who shared his policy beliefs—though not necessarily his ideological vision of governance.

What did that mean in practice? Basically, when Trump wanted to do self-destructive things, he was often either sidestepped or talked out of it by people who knew better. Special counsel Robert Muller’s report on the Russia investigation is a catalog of incidents where Trump asked aides to commit obstruction of justice or some other crime and they essentially ignored him. Trump threatened to close the U.S. border with Mexico to all trade at one point in 2019, only to back down after advisers warned him of the calamitous economic repercussions that would follow.

Other reversals foreshadowed his second-term mistakes. He constantly claimed that he would soon impose tariffs on all goods from China and from other countries as a negotiating cudgel, only to back down before doing so. After Iran shot down an unmanned U.S. drone in 2019, Trump threatened to “obliterate” Iran while his top aides pushed for diplomacy. “The United States is not looking to go to war with Iran,” then–Secretary of Defense Mark Esper said at the time.

Trump chafed at these restrictions, especially the ones that prevented him from exerting any direct control over the Justice Department. He fired Attorney General Jeff Sessions, his most ardent Cabinet supporter on anti-immigration policies, for recusing himself from the Russia investigation, which eventually led to the appointment of Mueller as special counsel. The president repeatedly pressured DOJ officials to cast doubt on the 2020 election results, which they refused to do. Those entreaties became part of the criminal case against Trump in 2023. (The Supreme Court had to invent new parts of the Constitution to save him from it.)

At least some voters cast ballots for Trump in 2024 hoping that electing him would magically make it February 2020 again, with no pandemic inflation but everything operating more or less the same. They drastically misread the political situation. Trump and his allies had spent the four-year wilderness crafting governance plans that would cut loose many of the restraints that bound the president during his first term. There would be no more deep-state bureaucrats undermining Trump’s agenda at federal agencies, they thought, or weak-willed warfighters who wouldn’t intimidate foreign adversaries. Only fervent loyalists would carry out the president’s will.

Now the Trump administration can’t seem to do anything right. The USS Abraham Lincoln spent so long stationed in the Persian Gulf this year that basic ship amenities began to fall apart and multiple sailors reportedly attempted suicide. The administration’s cuts to food safety inspections led to a nationwide cyclospora outbreak over the summer; Taylor Farms executives reportedly tried to delay a recall of its contaminated lettuce by calling the White House directly to ask for the president to intervene. That, apparently, is how the country works right now.

By far the worst thing that could happen to the Trump administration was also its greatest success. In early January, U.S. military forces extracted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from his palace in Caracas in a nighttime raid with no American casualties. He currently awaits trial for alleged narco-terrorism crimes, in New York City. The raid, from which Trump would have been dissuaded by more conscientious advisers, went better than anyone could have hoped. When Iranian protesters rose up against the government in Tehran the following spring, the administration—pushed by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu—saw an opportunity to do the same thing in the Middle East.

A more sober set of national security advisers would have warned Trump that attacking Iran would likely consolidate public support around the country’s beleaguered government. They might have pointed out that, if the attack didn’t succeed at overthrowing the government, the surviving leaders would be even more hard-line than their predecessors. They might even retaliate by attacking U.S. military bases in the region or U.S. civilians overseas. They could even try to cut off oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and destroy neighboring countries’ infrastructure.

Unfortunately for the world, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was at the helm of the Pentagon instead. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who was confirmed despite multiple allegations of sexual misconduct, had promised to end “wokeness” in the American military. This meant purging Black soldiers, firing a disproportionate number of women and minority generals and admirals, and blocking promotions for qualified officers who happened to not be white men. He also exonerated U.S. soldiers who committed war crimes against Native Americans in the nineteenth century and renamed military bases after Confederate leaders.

In between these adventures, Hegseth and Trump failed to overthrow the Iranian government by force, blew through most of the U.S. military’s stockpile of advanced munitions, and retreated from the constellation of military bases in the Persian Gulf to escape Iranian retaliation. Tehran now has its hand on the jugular vein of the global economy, and it shows no sign of relenting. In deference to how incredibly unpopularly a new war in the Middle East landed among American voters, Trump has held off on major strikes until after Election Day.

More than a few Trump voters in 2024 hoped that returning him to power would bring down the cost of groceries. It did not, and it could not. Trump began his second term by imposing hundreds of billions of dollars in tariffs on America’s top trading partners, ranging from China to the European Union. The president evinced no knowledge of how tariffs actually work. He consistently lied about who pays them—it’s American businesses and customers, not foreign governments—and how a trade deficit works.

Trumpism is not a protest against how the world works. It is a rejection of the very concept of knowing how the world works. Ignorance is a virtue, and knowledge is a vice. All that matters is what Trump thinks, regardless of whether it can be independently verified or held accountable. By electing Trump, many of his movement’s adherents hoped to prove that their lack of expertise was as good as any credential that some liberal egghead could obtain from a woke, biased university.

Now we are living through their dreams come true. Trump has waged war against the nation’s universities, with some close allies openly calling for the de-intellectualization of Americans because it would be beneficial for the GOP’s electoral chances. He has laid waste to our nation’s scientific and technological research infrastructure out of some obscene desire by apparatchiks like Russell Vought to wield ideological control over it. His administration has purged thousands of scientists, experts, and lawyers from the federal civil service because they refused to unfailingly carry out the president’s whims. An anti-vaxxer who has espoused eugenic sentiments now sits atop the nation’s public health infrastructure. It has been a two-year triumph for people who love to be wrong and can make themselves rich by doing it.

These actions have a dire cost for ordinary Americans, who are now on track to be poorer, sicker, and less educated at the end of Trump’s second term than they were before it. Even their “successes” are failures. In September, top Trump adviser Stephen Miller shared a graph on Twitter claiming that the country’s foreign-born population had dropped by 2.9 million over the past 18 months. “The first sustained negative migration in 100 years, and picking up speed,” he crowed. The graph also showed that the overall number of immigrants in the U.S. hadn’t dropped below the levels they were at in January 2024. In other words, the Trump administration has wrought all this damage and destroyed tens of thousands of immigrants’ lives to bring the number down to … Biden-era levels. They can’t even do mass deportations right.

Someday soon, a Republican presidential candidate will campaign on the premise that he can deliver the “good” parts of Trumpism without the collateral damage of its namesake’s mistakes. They will be lying. All of this damage flows naturally from an exaltation of ignorance and the demonization of expertise. They will merely be promising easy solutions to make a quick buck and hoping to outrun the harms they cause. Hopefully, future generations of Americans will see through the con more easily than past electorates.

items.title: Democrats Win Michigan Senate as Abdul El-Sayed Makes History
items.content_text:
Michigan voted to send Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to the Senate Tuesday night, making him the first Muslim senator.

El-Sayed beat Republican Mike Rogers with 51.89 percent of the vote, Decision Desk HQ projected, with 77 percent of the votes counted.

“You’ll notice I always say ‘Inshallah’ [God-willing],” El-Sayed said in his victory speech Tuesday evening. “Tonight, we can turn that ‘Inshallah’ into ‘Alhamdulillah’ [Praise Be to God].”

El-Sayed survived a brutal election campaign beginning with the state’s Democratic primary in which millions of dollars in outside money was spent to try to defeat him, particularly from donors and organizations affiliated with the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC.

In the end, El-Sayed’s message that money spent on the Iran war and on aid to Israel should be used to help struggling Americans propelled him to victory over Rogers. The former Detroit and Wayne County health commissioner also fought off Islamophobic attacks from Rogers, President Trump, and Vice President JD Vance.

“JD, habibi, there’s a delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January,” El-Sayed said in his victory speech.

Last month, a Republican plant at a Michigan town hall attempted to trip up El-Sayed by asking him to condemn the Muslim Brotherhood, only for El-Sayed to turn the tables on the questioner, and create a viral campaign moment about his allegiance to the Constitution.

President Clinton, who inspired El-Sayed to go into politics, went to Michigan to campaign for El-Sayed and condemned the Islamophobic attacks on him in a powerful speech in late October. Former President Obama also campaigned in Michigan for El-Sayed, as did Vice President Kamala Harris.

El-Sayed’s victory in a close battleground state that Trump won in 2024 is even more good news for Democrats’ control of the Senate, but also for whoever the Democratic nominee for president will be in 2028. In order for Democrats to take back the White House in two years, they will almost certainly need Michigan’s electoral votes.

This story has been updated.

items.title: Good Riddance to Susan Collins
items.content_text:
Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine has been unseated by Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, bringing an end to her decades-long stint as the “rubber stamp” for the GOP’s agenda.

Collins called Jackson to concede Tuesday evening, MS NOW and CNN reported, as Jackson led with 52.2 percent of the vote and the race had not yet been called.

Despite Collins’s attempts to distance herself from President Donald Trump on the campaign trail, it seems that there was no shaking the black mark of the president’s endorsement. “I hope she wins,” Trump said during an interview in August. “She’s a good person, actually.”

Jackson, a former state senator, replaced erstwhile Democratic nominee Graham Platner in July, and quickly mounted a campaign that focused on Collins’s failure to meaningfully challenge Trump’s disastrous agenda.

It’s been a tough year for the five-term senator. In September, it was reported that the FBI was investigating Collins for an alleged illegal pay-to-play scheme with a defense contractor—until the Trump administration killed the probe. Earlier this year, the 73-year-old lawmaker revealed that she’d been diagnosed with a condition called essential tremor, which causes shakiness in the voice and hands.

Collins’s defeat represents a crucial step toward Democrats reclaiming control of the Senate.

items.title: Democrats Send First Native Woman to Senate as They Win Another Seat
items.content_text:
Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan defeated Republican candidate Michele Tafoya in Minnesota’s Senate race.

Flanagan has defeated Tafoya 54 to 43 percent, with 72 percent of votes counted.

Flanagan will replace Democratic Senator Tina Smith, making her the first Native woman in the U.S. Senate. Flanagan has served as Minnesota’s lieutenant governor since 2018, making her the highest-ranking Native American elected to executive office, according to her official bio.

Tafoya, a former sportscaster, targeted Flanagan for serving under Governor Tim Walz, who has been accused by Republicans of overseeing sweeping, systemic social services fraud.

In reality, the right-wing fervor over fraud allegations in Minnesota is a fabrication designed to punish Democrats and antagonize immigrants. The state has previously investigated and prosecuted improper payments to childcare services, as well as unrelated high-profile fraud prosecutions involving other Minnesota social services. Similar accusations made by the Trump administration have already been debunked.

The two candidates also sparred over Operation Metro Surge, the sweeping immigration enforcement operation that tore apart communities across their state—and claimed the lives of two U.S. citizens. Tafoya had placed the blame on Walz for refusing to coordinate local and state agencies with federal law enforcement, while Flanagan argued for dismantling Immigration and Customs Enforcement altogether.

Tafoya’s defeat gives Democrats an even greater majority in the Senate.

items.title: Blue Texas Is Finally Here
items.content_text:
It’s official: Blexas is here.

In a shocking upset, both Republican Governor Greg Abbott and former Attorney General Ken Paxton were ousted by Democratic challengers Tuesday.

Gina Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than three decades on Tuesday, ousting Abbott, the Republican incumbent, who outspent her by tens of millions of dollars. Hinojosa’s victory makes her the state’s first Hispanic governor.

Meanwhile, James Talarico beat embattled Republican Ken Paxton, becoming the state’s first Democratic senator in 33 years. Talarico’s victory helped push Democrats to retake control of the U.S. Senate.

Hinojosa and Talarico have won a state that President Donald Trump won by 56 percent just two years ago.

items.title: Democrats Win Senate Majority in Huge Blow to Trump
items.content_text:
Democrats have retaken control of the Senate, loosening President Donald Trump’s control on the government.

As of this writing, the Democrats hold 51 seats to Republicans’ 39. Democrats flipped six seats from Republicans this election. There are still 10 seats left to be called.

Democrats have also taken control of the House of Representatives.

Ahead of the midterm elections Tuesday, Republicans held 53 Senate seats to Democrats’ 45, after gaining control of the Senate in a major upset in 2024. Recent polling suggested that the most critical toss-up Senate races would be extremely tight.

While America’s authoritarian era likely won’t end in a day, the results of the Senate midterm elections are a searing indictment of Republicans’ rule and the first two years of Trump’s second term.

items.title: Democrats Even Won a Senate Seat in Iowa—Shout-Out Josh Turek
items.content_text:
Iowa Democratic state Representative Josh Turek won his state’s Senate race Tuesday, defeating Republican Representative Ashley Hinson.

Turek beat Hinson 51 to 45, at 79 percent of precincts reporting, according to Decision Desk HQ. He will replace retiring GOP Senator Joni Ernst.

Democrats have not won a Senate race in Iowa since 2008. Turek’s victory pushed Democrats closer to regaining control of the U.S. Senate.

Hinson, a Republican, widely supports President Donald Trump’s political agenda. Over the weekend, Trump campaigned in support of Hinson, where he ranted about her weight loss.

items.title: Democrats Win Kansas Senate Election for First Time in 94 Years
items.content_text:
Kansans have just elected a Democratic senator for the first time since 1932.

Pastor Adam Hamilton beat incumbent Senator Roger Marshall 53 to 44, Decision Desk HQ reported, with 83 percent of votes counted.

Hamiton’s stunning upset happened in large part thanks to President Trump and the GOP’s record unpopularity. It didn’t hurt that Marshall, a doctor before entering politics, was haunted by his record of suing patients who couldn’t pay their medical bills, sometimes for as little as $101.

Marshall’s low poll numbers had prompted Trump and Vice President JD Vance to campaign for him in the state, which may have hurt his chances even further. Marshall tried to distance himself from some of Trump’s more unpopular policies, criticizing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in September, but it wasn’t enough. Marshall’s campaign had other missteps, like when he used unapproved pictures of children in an attack ad against Hamilton. Trump also used an antisemitic slur to defend Marshall against the attacks on his patient lawsuits only two weeks before the election.

Ultimately, Hamilton’s moral message won out. At a debate with Marshall in September, the pastor said, “There are 2,000 verses in the Bible that speak to caring for the poor. That is not happening with this man.” Hamilton will join Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock, who was previously the only other Democratic pastor in the Senate.

items.title: Democrats Win Ohio Governor’s Race as Vivek Ramaswamy Blows It Again
items.content_text:
Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio’s gubernatorial election Tuesday and will become the first Democratic governor in the state in 15 years.

Ramaswamy, a pharmaceutical executive who previously ran for president in 2024, lost by about 4 percent in a state that voted for President Trump in the past three presidential elections with increasing margins.

After he easily won the Republican primary in May, Ramaswamy made a series of missteps in his general election campaign. These included getting booed off the stage at a libertarian student group’s national convention in Cleveland in July, posting (and then deleting) a widely-mocked video of himself at a batting cage, nearly dropping a 10-year-old boy he inexplicably picked up at a rally last month, and deciding to feature a convicted sex offender in an October campaign ad.

But Ramaswamy’s most egregious error was enlisting Acton’s estranged mother Donna Arthur in a campaign ad calling the Democrat a liar just weeks ago. Arthur stayed with her husband, Cledith Arthur, even after he was tried and convicted for sexually abusing 12-year-old Acton, leading to their estrangement. As the ad brought widespread backlash from Democrats and Republicans, Ramaswamy doubled down, with Vice President JD Vance and Trump coming to his defense.

That proved to sink Ramaswamy’s chances and deliver victory to Acton, a doctor and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, in a state where Democrats have been losing ground for more than a decade. Now,the state will be closely watched to see if Democrats can flip it again in two years when Ohio native Vance will likely be running for president.

items.title: This Blue Wave Is the Beginning of the End for Trump
items.content_text:
Two years ago, it looked like Donald Trump had a mandate. He had returned to power after attempting a coup in 2021 and then, just five months before the 2024 election, being convicted of dozens of felonies related to the Stormy Daniels hush-money scheme. And somehow, despite this flagrant lawlessness, he had won more convincingly than ever before, winning not only the Electoral College but also, for the first time, the popular vote, thanks in part to unprecedented gains with Black, Latino, and young voters, particularly men. It wasn’t just a political victory, either: Star athletes began celebrating scores with the “Trump dance.” He wasn’t just normalized. He was American culture.

Or so it seemed at the time. That conclusion had already aged poorly before this week, but Tuesday’s election results make it look ridiculous. What we are seeing almost defies description. South Carolina and Texas will soon have Democratic senators. So will Kansas. Georgia just elected the country’s first-ever Black woman governor. There are many explanations for this blue tsunami—Iran, tariffs, horrific GOP candidate selection—but the simplest is also the most persuasive: This is a historic rebuke of Donald Trump and his party.

Far from being the dawn of a new political epoch, Trump’s return to power was something closer to a flash in the pan. By last summer, he had squandered what little political capital he had entered office with. And now, he will have to deal with a Democratic House and a Democratic Senate. There will be investigations. There will be accountability. And there will likely be a furious, perhaps unprecedented response from the president and the MAGA loyalists who surround him. But make no mistake: Trump’s downfall has begun. The only question is what happens to the political movement he has led for the last 11 years.

Trump, it turns out, had not really won hearts and minds in 2024. He won because Joe Biden had overseen a period of rampant inflation, which was not his fault, and had held onto a doomed reelection campaign despite widespread concerns about his age, which was. Trump’s victory two years ago, in retrospect, was a massive, foolish risk by voters that he would govern more or less like he did during the pre-Covid period of his first term, which is to say erratically but not destructively.

Those of us who saw Trump’s victory in sweeping cultural terms were wrong. But that is also how those surrounding him saw his victory—and they promptly overplayed their hand. They should have understood their mandate as largely limited to bringing down soaring costs. Instead, they eviscerated the federal government. They invaded U.S. cities with masked goons. They deported law-abiding immigrants and murdered U.S. citizens seeking to protect them. They started two wars—one economic, the other literal—that caused prices, which the Biden administration had just started to bring under control, to soar again.

This administration has been lawless, authoritarian, imperial, fascistic, and plutocratic. There is no question that is the most corrupt in American history. The president and his cronies have lined their pockets while the cost of basic commodities has skyrocketed. They have attempted to cover up the president’s ties to the pedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein, while defying court orders and launching bogus, retaliatory, politically motivated prosecutions. They will say that the Democrats “stole” this election. But they only have themselves to blame.

What is undoubtedly true is that we have seen the MAGA agenda in its clearest realization these last two years. No future Republican can say, as some said of Reaganism after Ronald Reagan left office, that real Trumpism has never been tried. We have seen MAGA in all its glory—or rather, horror.

It is tempting, given how completely Trump has sabotaged his second term, to discount the Democrats’ achievement this week. It is certainly true that most of the responsibility lies at Trump’s feet. It is also true that this has been an unusually chaotic primary cycle, one that didn’t exactly suggest that the Democrats have learned hard truths from their stint in the political wilderness. The blue wave arrived after quite a bit of teeth-grinding anxiety, particularly in Senate races in Maine, Michigan, and Alaska. And yet, the Democrats won those first two states; the third has yet to be called. The picture is clear: Voters have showed up everywhere, in extraordinary numbers, to vote against the revolution that Trump and his backers thought they were leading. That revolution is dead now.

The optimistic take is that some of that chaos is the result of what amounts to political growing pains. Democrats have embraced new candidates and new positions. They are figuring out how to move with an electorate that is rapidly evolving on a host of issues, from the support of Israel to trans rights. But the larger takeaway from the midterms is that voters were willing to back practically anyone with a (D) next to their name. If the party is still figuring out precisely where it stands on thorny issues, there is time to figure that out. Right now, the Democratic tent is as large as it has been in a generation.

Democrats will soon have a national stage to debate where the party should stand on key issues—not only because they will take control of the House and Senate, but because the jockeying for the party’s presidential nomination will begin very shortly. For the first time since 2008, there is not a clear establishment-backed candidate waiting in the wings—unless you count Kamala Harris, who lost badly to Trump and may not run again (she shouldn’t).

Meanwhile, the Republicans will be doing something even harder: figuring out who they are without Trump. And they will have to do that while Trump is still around. On the one hand, he’s a lame-duck president who may spend the rest of his time in office raving about men’s asses and his interior decorating projects. On the other hand, Trump is a megalomaniac with a deep fear of irrelevance, so he will do whatever he can to strengthen his grip on the Republican Party and try to influence where it goes after he’s whisked away from his brand-new helipad for the final time.

In the history of American politics, there has never been a problem quite like the one Republicans are facing now. For the last decade, they have allowed their party to transform into a cult of personality. Trump has had almost total control over the GOP at almost every level, and has remade the party in his own image. Now, voters have delivered a historic rebuke to that party. Ordinarily, you would expect members of that party to reject the massively incompetent and destructive person who has led it for three consecutive presidential cycles. You would expect them to learn lessons from their defeat and to start to rebuild. But that is simply not possible with Trump, who will not allow Republicans to reject him.

Over the next two years, the Democrats can continue to build on the message that helped return them to power on Tuesday—one that centers Trump’s corruption and incompetence. They will do so as evidence of that corruption and incompetence continues to mount, and they now have power they can wield to investigate it. But even though Republicans have lost power in Congress, and Trump is historically unpopular, he is still in charge. He is also venal, thin-skinned, and increasingly erratic. The next two years will be turbulent. They may even be scary. But for now, let us take comfort in this much: Two years ago, Trump thought he was invincible. This week, the Democrats shoved his political mortality in his face.

items.title: Republicans Have Total Meltdown Over the Blue Wave—and It’s Delicious
items.content_text:
The blue wave is here, and Republicans aren’t taking it very well.

As Democrats began notching huge midterm victories on Tuesday, including winning back control of the House of Representatives and securing key victories in races across the nation, Republicans saw the writing on the wall.

Politico reported that senior Republican Party members are particularly worried about Florida, where Republican Ashley Moody won the Senate race against Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist, by just three percentage points.

“Florida is bad. Real bad,” one strategist said.

“A socialist is on track to win Miami-Dade County, where most of the voters fled literal socialism and still refused to vote for Republicans. If that doesn’t tell you how big of a colossal fuck up the first two years of Trump 2.0 was I don’t know what will,” said another.

“It’s a ruby-red state. If we have problems there, we have real issues,” an adviser said.

MAGA commentators also spent Tuesday night publicly lamenting their party’s poor initial midterm showings, which indicate a rejection of President Trump’s larger political movement in general.

“This isn’t a blue tsunami. This is a blue great mud flood,” wrote right-wing podcaster Tim Pool. “Shit. Its almost like the GOP campaigned on nothing and deserve to get blown out. Fucking insane.”

“Tonight should be a wake-up call. The next two years cannot be more speeches, more promises, and more excuses for why nothing gets done,” former Trump national security adviser Michael Flynn wrote on Truth Social. “People are tired of voting for change and then being told to wait until the next election. If we put you in office, we expect you to do the job. Tell us what you’ve accomplished, where you’ve fallen short, and what you’re doing about it. Having an R next to your name does not get you a pass.... The next two years need to be about accountability. We cannot afford to be having this same conversation in 2028.”

items.title: James Talarico Becomes First Democratic Senator in Texas in 33 Years
items.content_text:
James Talarico has officially turned Texas blue for the first time in 33 years.

Talarico beat embattled former Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton 58–40 with 68 percent of the vote counted, the Decision Desk HQ reported.

Talarico thus wins a state that President Trump won by 56 percent just two years ago. The Presbyterian former House member ran on a progressive populist platform consisting of affordability, economic inequality, political corruption, and health care reform.

Paxton did just about everything he could to lose this race. From his indictment and suspension to his alleged affair and subsequent divorce, his misuse of taxpayer funds for vacations, to his controversial, leak-filled Senate campaign, Trump could not have picked a more vulnerable candidate to loosen the GOP’s grip on the Lone Star state.

items.title: Democrats Win South Carolina Senate as Lindsey Graham’s Sister Flops
items.content_text:
South Carolinian voters weren’t in the mood for groundless nepotism this election season.

Acting South Carolina Senator Darline Graham, the younger sister of the late Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat Annie Andrews Tuesday.

Andrews beat Graham 51.1 to 47 percent, Decision Desk HQ projected.

The junior Graham took the reins of her sibling’s powerful office in July, days after the 71-year-old suddenly passed away from an aortic dissection. Despite having zero relevant experience or qualifications, Graham gained the president’s endorsement and was subsequently appointed by South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster. She then defied Republican strategists by throwing her hat in the GOP primary ring the following month, besting Representative Ralph Norman, a five-term lawmaker who has represented the Palmetto State in various legislative capacities since 2005.

But voters were apparently unimpressed by Graham’s four-month tenure in office. At the onset, Graham promised to follow in her brother’s footsteps, aligning herself with the MAGA movement and its various policy points. But her ignorance quickly shone through.

During her primary debates, Graham flopped on a softball debate question regarding Taiwan, confessing that “national security is not my thing.” In the same debate, she forgot the population of her own state, falsely claiming that South Carolina’s population is 50 million people—more than New York and Florida combined. Fact check: The state population is less than six million people.

Andrews’s win marks the first time since 2005 that a Democrat has represented South Carolina in the Senate, and the first time that a woman earned the electorate’s vote for the coveted position.

items.title: Republicans’ Attempt to Rig the Map Backfires Big-Time in Florida
items.content_text:
It looks like Republicans have just played themselves in Florida. As midterm election results rolled in Tuesday night, it quickly became clear that GOP gerrymandering in the Sunshine State had seriously backfired.

Democrat Kathy Castor held onto her seat in Florida’s 14th congressional district, fending off a challenge from Republican Mike Beltran. Republicans purposefully redrew that district to get rid of Castor, by including a lot less of Tampa and a lot more of its outlying rural counties. In 2024, President Donald Trump won the areas making up this new district by 11 points.

In Florida’s 22nd congressional district, Democrat Pia Dandiya defeated Republican Casey Askar, after Governor Ron DeSantis’s gerrymandering efforts created an open seat for the Republicans to steal. The state’s current 22nd district is represented by Democrat Lois Frankel, who is now running in its 23rd district.

In the race for Florida’s Senate seat, Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist, was defeated by Republican incumbent Ashley Moody—but when the race was called at 84.3 percent of the vote reported, Moody led Nixon by only 0.7 percentage points. The Republican won, but not by nearly as much as expected for a historically red state.

items.title: Democrats Take Control of the House of Representatives
items.content_text:
Democrats are projected to retake control of the House of Representatives for the first time in four years.

Decision Desk HQ projected Democrats will seize the chamber from Republicans. It is not yet clear which party has taken control of the Senate.

Republicans gained control of the House two years ago during the 2022 midterm elections. While there was no “red wave” as widely predicted, Republicans were able to flip 19 districts from blue to red.

Ahead of the midterm elections Tuesday, Republicans held only a slim four-seat majority over Democrats. The latest polls had heavily indicated that Democrats would retake control of the House.

While America’s authoritarian era likely won’t end in a day, the results of the House midterm elections are a searing indictment on Republicans’ rule and the first two years of Trump’s second term.

items.title: Leaked Texts Expose GOP in Key Swing State Bracing for Disaster
items.content_text:
Midterm election predictions are not looking good for Republicans in battleground states.

Garrett Archer, a data analyst for an Arizona ABC News affiliate, shared messages Tuesday from an unnamed GOP analyst that don’t bode well for their party.

“God all my models are already projecting doom. And it’s 8am,” the text messages read.

Conservative campaigns around the country are feeling similar pressure as their candidates were forced to thread the needle between kowtowing to the president’s fragile ego and distancing themselves from his wildly unpopular military and economic policies.

Politico reported Friday that some Republicans are bracing for “a brutal evening,” expecting major losses in both chambers of Congress.

“Once the dominoes start falling it becomes hard to stop them,” a senior GOP strategist told the newsroom.

Donald Trump has already started surveying the landscape of his Cabinet for potential fall guys should the elections go south. Last month, Trump reportedly called several close confidants to assess the job performance of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, his former campaign manager and famed “Ice Maiden,” as a potential scapegoat for a major midterm bust. He’s also made the rounds to assess current attitudes about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine as the Iran war drags on into its eighth month.

Republicans, meanwhile, know exactly where to point their fingers.

“We all know who the problem is. It’s Trump,” a GOP strategist involved in midterm races across the country told Politico Monday.

That same strategist was unsure about how the Republican Party might reform itself if the party sustains major losses on Tuesday.

“Look, a lot of Republicans have held their tongues. A lot of Republicans who have real problems with the way things have gone the last two years have been good soldiers,” they said. “But what happens if we lose 35 House seats and six Senate seats?”

items.title: Trump DOJ Targets Democrats in Senate Race Probe Right Before Election
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump is taking drastic steps to investigate Alaska’s Senate election, with the Department of Justice sending criminal target letters to about 20 leading Democrats.

The New York Times reported on Election Day that Marc Elias, a Democratic elections lawyer whose firm represents Alaska Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola, has received a letter. So has at least one official at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. The letters tell the recipients that they could be targets in the DOJ’s investigation into the recruitment of a candidate with the same name as incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.

The DOJ is investigating possible donor fraud and conspiracy charges as well, an anonymous source told the Times. According to the publication, it’s not known when the letters were sent or if every intended recipient got them.

Trump has been raving about the Alaska contest for days, accusing the Democratic Party of election fraud and repeatedly attacking Elias and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. Trump told Fox & Friends Tuesday morning that Elias “was a bad guy, very bad guy” who “should go to jail, in my opinion.”

On Monday night, Trump made a series of Truth Social posts claiming that independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan was “missing in action” and suggesting that he had been kidnapped. He speculated that “the Dumocrats are trying to steal this Race by putting a FAKE Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr. on the Ballot. People will not be able to figure it out, and many Votes will be lost.”

That, along with the target letters, could be a hint that Trump will try to take action in the event that Peltola wins the race. He’s openly said that he would consider a “redo” of the election if that happens, although he lacks the legal backing to make such a move, especially considering Alaska has ranked-choice voting. He’d end up sowing confusion and undermining confidence not just in Alaska, but in the entire country.

items.title: Google Tries to Blackmail Schools Into Using Its AI Tools
items.content_text:
Schools that reject Google’s AI services apparently won’t be allowed to use Google at all.

The company announced Tuesday that it will turn off search engine access for K-12 schools that toggle off its AI tools as soon as next year. Google executives claim the decision is based on the technologies’ recent fusion.

“Search and AI are deeply integrated,” Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times, adding that students at schools that have banned AI “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Many schools across the country have already invested in Google’s technologies, purchasing low-cost Google Chromebooks to assist educational instruction. Beyond that, Google’s search algorithm has led the industry for the last two decades, besting its competitors to the point that its mere name has become synonymous with research.

Lina Khan, the former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, argued in a statement on X that Google had used its “search monopoly to coerce schools” into adopting AI tools. She noted Google has been found legally liable multiple times for antitrust law violations.

“This latest move shows it remains unchastened,” Khan wrote. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools … Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

Studies conducted over the last several months have indicated that the risks attached to the use of AI in schools outweigh the potential benefits. A January report by the Brookings Institution’s Center for Universal Education found that AI can “undermine children’s foundational development,” and that “the damages it has already caused are daunting.”
